entries.32d8f56c32a3b8a2e927fe3d9e56691b23ef5e87: <div sID="gen10140" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="36" osisID="Job.36" sID="Job.36"/> <div eID="gen10140" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10141" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen10142" type="x-p"/> Elihu, having largely reproved Job for some of his unadvised speeches, which Job had nothing to say in the vindication of, here comes more generally to set him to rights in his notions of God's dealings with him. His other friends had stood to it that, because he was a wicked man, therefore his afflictions were so great and so long. But Elihu only maintained that the affliction was sent for his trial, and that therefore it was lengthened out because Job was not, as yet, thoroughly humbled under it, nor had duly accommodated himself to it. He urges many reasons, taken from the wisdom and righteousness of God, his care of his people, and especially his greatness and almighty power, with which, in this and the following chapter, he persuades him to submit to the hand of God. Here we have, I. His preface, <reference osisRef="Job.36.2-Job.36.4">ver. 2-4</reference>. II. The account he gives of the methods of God's providence towards the children of men, according as they conduct themselves, <reference osisRef="Job.36.5-Job.36.15">ver. 5-15</reference>. III. The fair warning and good counsel he gives to Job thereupon, <reference osisRef="Job.36.16-Job.36.21">ver. 16-21</reference>. IV. His demonstration of God's sovereignty and omnipotence, which he gives instances of in the operations of common providence, and which is a reason why we should all submit to him in his dealings with us, <reference osisRef="Job.36.22-Job.36.33">ver. 22-33</reference>. This he prosecutes and enlarges upon in the following chapter.
entries.9e9943b9f839c17f71a698b4a1e6048bca04e74b: <div eID="gen10142" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen10141" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Address of Elihu. (<hi type="small-caps">b. c.</hi> 1520.)</title> <div sID="gen10143" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Elihu also proceeded, and said, <hi type="super">2</hi> Suffer me a little, and I will show thee that <hi type="italic">I have</hi> yet to speak on God's behalf. <hi type="super">3</hi> I will fetch my knowledge from afar, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker. <hi type="super">4</hi> For truly my words <hi type="italic">shall</hi> not <hi type="italic">be</hi> false: he that is perfect in knowledge <hi type="italic">is</hi> with thee. <div eID="gen10143" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10144" type="x-p"/> Once more Elihu begs the patience of the auditory, and Job's particularly, for he has not said all that he has to say, but he will not detain them long. <hi type="italic">Stand about me a little</hi> (so some read it), <reference osisRef="Job.36.2">v. 2</reference>. "Let me have your attendance, your attention, awhile longer, and I will speak but this once, as plainly and as much to the purpose as I can." To gain this he pleads, 1. That he had a good cause, and a noble and very fruitful subject: <hi type="italic">I have yet to speak on God's behalf.</hi> He spoke as an advocate for God, and therefore might justly expect the ear of the court. Some indeed pretend to speak on God's behalf who really speak for themselves; but those who sincerely appear in the cause of God, and speak in behalf of his honour, his truths, his ways, his people, shall be sure neither to want instructions (<hi type="italic">it shall be given them in that same hour what they shall speak</hi>) nor to lose their cause or their fee. Nor need they fear lest they should exhaust their subject. Those that have spoken ever so much may yet find more to be spoken on God's behalf. 2. That he had something to offer that was uncommon, and out of the road of vulgar observation: <hi type="italic">I will fetch my knowledge from afar</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.36.3">v. 3</reference>), that is, "we will have recourse to our first principles and the highest notions we can make use of to serve any purpose." It is worth while to go far for this knowledge of God, to dig for it, to travel for it; it will recompense our pains, and, though far-fetched, is not dear-bought. 3. That his design was undeniably honest; for all he aimed at was to ascribe righteousness to his Maker, to maintain and clear this truth, that God is righteous in all his ways. In speaking of God, and speaking for him, it is good to remember that he is our Maker, to call him so, and therefore to be ready to do him and the interests of his kingdom the best service we can. If he be our Maker, we have our all from him, must use our all for him, and be very jealous for his honour. That his management should be very just and fair (<reference osisRef="Job.36.4">v. 4</reference>): "<hi type="italic">My words shall not be false,</hi> neither disagreeable to the thing itself nor to my own thoughts and apprehensions. It is truth that I am contending for, and that for truth's sake, with all possible sincerity and plainness." He will make use of plain and solid arguments and not the subtleties and niceties of the schools. "He who is perfect or upright in knowledge is now reasoning with thee; and therefore let him not only have a fair hearing, but let what he says be taken in good part, as meant well." The perfection of our knowledge in this world is to be honest and sincere in searching out truth, in applying it to ourselves, and in making use of what we know for the good of others.
entries.6775ad654d83a12ceb18f7e73acb17b8d4fdeb0b: <div eID="gen10144" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10145" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">5</hi> Behold, God <hi type="italic">is</hi> mighty, and despiseth not <hi type="italic">any: he is</hi> mighty in strength <hi type="italic">and</hi> wisdom. <hi type="super">6</hi> He preserveth not the life of the wicked: but giveth right to the poor. <hi type="super">7</hi> He withdraweth not his eyes from the righteous: but with kings <hi type="italic">are they</hi> on the throne; yea, he doth establish them for ever, and they are exalted. <hi type="super">8</hi> And if <hi type="italic">they be</hi> bound in fetters, <hi type="italic">and</hi> be holden in cords of affliction; 9 Then he showeth them their work, and their transgressions that they have exceeded. <hi type="super">10</hi> He openeth also their ear to discipline, and commandeth that they return from iniquity. <hi type="super">11</hi> If they obey and serve <hi type="italic">him,</hi> they shall spend their days in prosperity, and their years in pleasures. <hi type="super">12</hi> But if they obey not, they shall perish by the sword, and they shall die without knowledge. <hi type="super">13</hi> But the hypocrites in heart heap up wrath: they cry not when he bindeth them. <hi type="super">14</hi> They die in youth, and their life <hi type="italic">is</hi> among the unclean. <div eID="gen10145" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10146" type="x-p"/> Elihu, being to speak on God's behalf, and particularly to ascribe righteousness to his Maker, here shows that the disposals of divine Providence are all, not only according to the eternal counsels of his will, but according to the eternal rules of equity. God acts as a righteous governor, for, <div eID="gen10146" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10147" type="x-p"/> I. He does not think it below him to take notice of the meanest of his subjects, nor does poverty or obscurity set any at a distance from his favour. If men are mighty, they are apt to look with a haughty disdain upon those that are not of distinction and make no figure; but <hi type="italic">God is mighty,</hi> infinitely so, and yet he <hi type="italic">despises not any,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.5">v. 5</reference>. He humbles himself to take cognizance of the affairs of the meanest, to do them justice and to show them kindness. Job thought himself and his cause slighted because God did not immediately appear for him. "No," says Elihu, <hi type="italic">God despises not any,</hi> which is a good reason why we should honour all men. <hi type="italic">He is mighty in strength and wisdom,</hi> and yet does not look with contempt upon those that have but a little strength and wisdom, if they but mean honestly. Nay, for this reason he despises not any, because his wisdom and strength are incontestably infinite and therefore the condescensions of his grace can be no diminution to him. Those that are wise and good will not look upon any with scorn and disdain. <div eID="gen10147" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10148" type="x-p"/> II. He gives no countenance to the greatest, if they be bad (<reference osisRef="Job.36.6">v. 6</reference>): <hi type="italic">He preserves not the life of the wicked.</hi> Though their life may be prolonged, yet not under any special care of the divine Providence, but only its common protection. Job had said that <hi type="italic">the wicked live, become old, and are mighty in power,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.7">ch. xxi. 7</reference>. "No," says Elihu: "he seldom suffers wicked men to become old. He preserves not their life so long as they expected, nor with that comfort and satisfaction which are indeed our life; and their preservation is but a reservation for the day of wrath," <reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Rom. ii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen10148" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10149" type="x-p"/> III. He is always ready to right those that are any way injured, and to plead their cause (<reference osisRef="Job.36.6">v. 6</reference>): He <hi type="italic">gives right to the poor,</hi> avenges their quarrel upon their persecutors and forces them to make restitution of what they have robbed them of. If men will not right the injured poor, God will. <div eID="gen10149" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10150" type="x-p"/> IV. He takes a particular care for the protection of his good subjects, <reference osisRef="Job.36.7">v. 7</reference>. He not only looks on them, but he never looks off them: <hi type="italic">He withdraws not his eyes from the righteous.</hi> Though they may seem sometimes neglected and forgotten, and that befals them which looks like an oversight of Providence, yet tender careful eye of their heavenly Father never withdraws from them. If our eye be ever towards God in duty, his eye will be ever upon us in mercy, and, when we are at the lowest, will not overlook us. <div eID="gen10150" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10151" type="x-p"/> 1. Sometimes he prefers good people to places of trust and honour (<reference osisRef="Job.36.7">v. 7</reference>): <hi type="italic">With kings are</hi> they <hi type="italic">on the throne,</hi> and every sheaf is made to bow to theirs. When righteous persons are advanced to places of honour and power, it is in mercy to them; for God's grace in them will both arm them against the temptations that attend preferment and enable them to improve the opportunity it gives them of doing good. It is also in mercy to those over whom they are set: <hi type="italic">When the righteous bear rule the city rejoices.</hi> If the righteous be advanced, they are established. Those that in honour keep a good conscience stand upon sure ground, and high places are not such slippery ground to them as they are to others. But, because it is not often that we see good men made great men in this world, this may be supposed to refer to the honour to which the righteous shall rise when their Redeemer shall <hi type="italic">stand at the latter day upon the earth;</hi> for then only they shall be exalted for ever, and established for ever; then shall they all shine forth as the sun, and be made kings and priests to our God. <div eID="gen10151" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10152" type="x-p"/> 2. If at any time he bring them into affliction, it is for the good of their souls, <reference osisRef="Job.36.8-Job.36.10">v. 8-10</reference>. Some good people are preferred to honour and power, but others are in trouble. Now observe, (1.) The distress supposed (<reference osisRef="Job.36.8">v. 8</reference>): <hi type="italic">If they be bound in fetters,</hi> laid in prison as Joseph was, or <hi type="italic">holden in the cords of</hi> any other <hi type="italic">affliction,</hi> confined by pain and sickness, hampered by poverty, bound in their counsels, and, notwithstanding all their struggles, held long in this distress. This was Job's case; he was caught, and kept fast, <hi type="italic">in the cords of anguish</hi> (as some read it); but observe, (2.) The design God has, in bringing his people into such distresses as these; it is for the benefit of their souls, the consideration of which should reconcile us to affliction and make us think well of it. Three things God intends when he afflicts us:—[1.] To discover past sins to us, and to bring them to our remembrance. Then he shows them that amiss in them which before they did not see. He discovers to them the fact of sin: <hi type="italic">He shows them their work.</hi> Sin is our own work. If there be any good in us, it is God's work; and we are concerned to see what work we have made by sin. He discovers the fault of sin, shows them <hi type="italic">their transgressions</hi> of the law of God, and withal the sinfulness of sin, <hi type="italic">that they have exceeded,</hi> and have been beyond measure sinful. True penitents lay a load upon themselves, do not extenuate, but aggravate, their sins, and own that they have exceeded in them. Affliction sometimes answers to the sin; it serves, however, to awaken the conscience and puts men upon considering. [2.] To dispose our hearts to receive present instructions: Then <hi type="italic">he opens their ear to discipline,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.10">v. 10</reference>. Whom God chastens <hi type="italic">he teaches</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Ps. xciv. 12</reference>), and the affliction makes people willing to learn, softens the wax, that it may receive the impression of the seal; yet it does not do this of itself, but the grace of God working with and by it; it is he that opens the ear, that opens the heart, who has the key of David. [3.] To deter and draw us off from iniquity for the future. This is the errand on which the affliction is sent; it is a command to <hi type="italic">return from iniquity,</hi> to have no more to do with sin, to turn from it with an aversion to it and a resolution never to return to it any more, <reference osisRef="Hos.14.8">Hos. xiv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen10152" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10153" type="x-p"/> 3. If the affliction do its work, and accomplish that for which it is sent, he will comfort them again, according to the time that he has afflicted them (<reference osisRef="Job.36.11">v. 11</reference>): <hi type="italic">If they obey and serve him,</hi>—if they comply with his design and serve his purpose in these dispensations,—if, when the affliction is removed, they continue in the same good mind that they were in when they were under the smart of it and perform the vows they made then,—if they live in obedience to God's commands, particularly those which relate to his service and worship, and in all instances make conscience of their duty to him,—then <hi type="italic">they shall spend their days in prosperity</hi> again <hi type="italic">and their years in</hi> true <hi type="italic">pleasures.</hi> Piety is the only sure way to prosperity and pleasure; this is a certain truth, and yet few will believe it. If we faithfully serve God, (1.) We have the promise of outward prosperity, the promise of the life that now is, and the comforts of it, as far as is for God's glory and our good; and who would desire them any further? (2.) We have the possession of inward pleasures, the comfort of communion with God and a good conscience, and that great peace which those have that love God's law. If we rejoice not in the Lord always, and in hope of eternal life, it is our own fault; and what better pleasures can we spend our years in? <div eID="gen10153" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10154" type="x-p"/> 4. If the affliction do not do its work, let them expect the furnace to be heated seven times hotter till they are consumed (<reference osisRef="Job.36.12">v. 12</reference>): <hi type="italic">If they obey not,</hi> if they are not bettered by their afflictions, are not reclaimed and reformed, they shall perish by the sword of God's wrath. Those whom his rod does not cure his sword will kill; and the consuming fire will prevail if the refining fire do not; for when God judges he will overcome. If <hi type="italic">Ahaz, in his distress, trespass yet more against the Lord, this is that king Ahaz</hi> that is marked for ruin, <reference osisRef="2Chr.28.22">2 Chron. xxviii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.29-Jer.6.30">Jer. vi. 29, 30</reference>. God would have instructed them by their afflictions, but they received not instruction, would not take the hints that were given them; and therefore <hi type="italic">they shall die without knowledge,</hi> ere they are aware, without any further previous notices given them; or <hi type="italic">they shall die because they were without knowledge</hi> notwithstanding the means of knowledge which they were blessed with. Those that <hi type="italic">die without knowledge</hi> die without grace and are undone for ever. <div eID="gen10154" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10155" type="x-p"/> V. He brings ruin upon hypocrites, the secret enemies of his kingdom (such as Elihu described, <reference osisRef="Job.36.12">v. 12</reference>), who, though they were numbered among the righteous whom Elihu had spoken of before, yet did not obey God, but, being children of disobedience and darkness, become children of wrath and perdition; these are the <hi type="italic">hypocrites in heart, who heap up wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.13">v. 13</reference>. See the nature of hypocrisy: it lies in the heart, which is for the world and the flesh when the outside seems to be for God and religion. Many that are saints in show and saints in word are hypocrites in heart. That spring is corrupt, and there is an evil treasure there. See the mischievousness of hypocrisy: hypocrites <hi type="italic">heap up wrath.</hi> They are doing that every day which is provoking to God, and will be reckoned with for it all together in the great day. <hi type="italic">They treasure up wrath against the day of wrath,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Rom. ii. 5</reference>. Their sins are <hi type="italic">laid up in store with God among his treasures,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.32.34">Deut. xxxii. 34. </reference>Compare <reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">Jam. v. 3</reference>. As what goes up a vapour comes down a shower, so what goes up sin, if not repented of, will come down wrath. They think they are heaping up wealth, heaping up merits, but, when the treasures are opened, it will prove they were heaping up wrath. Observe, 1. What they do to heap up wrath. What is it that is so provoking? It is this, <hi type="italic">They cry not when he binds them,</hi> that is, when they are in affliction, bound with the cords of trouble, their hearts are hardened, they are stubborn and unhumbled, and will not cry to God nor make their application to him. They are stupid and senseless as stocks and stones, despising the chastening of the Lord. 2. What are the effects of that wrath? <hi type="italic">They die in youth, and their life is among the unclean,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.14">v. 14</reference>. This is the portion of hypocrites, whom Christ denounced many woes against. If they continue impenitent, (1.) They shall die a sudden death, <hi type="italic">die in youth,</hi> when death is most a surprise, and death (that is, the consequence of it) is always such to hypocrites; as those that die in youth die when they hoped to live, so hypocrites, at death, go to hell, when they hoped to go to heaven. <hi type="italic">When a wicked man dies his expectations shall perish.</hi> (2.) They shall die the second death. <hi type="italic">Their life,</hi> after death (for so it comes in here), <hi type="italic">is among the unclean,</hi> among the <hi type="italic">fornicators</hi> (so some), among the worst and vilest of sinners, notwithstanding their specious and plausible profession. It is among the <hi type="italic">Sodomites</hi> (so the margin), those filthy wretches, who <hi type="italic">going after strange flesh, are set forth for an example, suffering the vengeance of eternal fire,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jude.1.7">Jude 7</reference>. The souls of the wicked live after death, but they live among the unclean, the unclean spirits, the devil and his angels, forever separated from the new Jerusalem, into which <hi type="italic">no unclean thing shall enter.</hi>
entries.fb3ba74233cf7b75abae308f19022cc40a0a219e: <div eID="gen10155" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10156" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">15</hi> He delivereth the poor in his affliction, and openeth their ears in oppression. <hi type="super">16</hi> Even so would he have removed thee out of the strait <hi type="italic">into</hi> a broad place, where <hi type="italic">there is</hi> no straitness; and that which should be set on thy table <hi type="italic">should be</hi> full of fatness. <hi type="super">17</hi> But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked: judgment and justice take hold <hi type="italic">on thee.</hi> <hi type="super">18</hi> Because <hi type="italic">there is</hi> wrath, <hi type="italic">beware</hi> lest he take thee away with <hi type="italic">his</hi> stroke: then a great ransom cannot deliver thee. <hi type="super">19</hi> Will he esteem thy riches? <hi type="italic">no,</hi> not gold, nor all the forces of strength. <hi type="super">20</hi> Desire not the night, when people are cut off in their place. 21 Take heed, regard not iniquity: for this hast thou chosen rather than affliction. <hi type="super">22</hi> Behold, God exalteth by his power: who teacheth like him? <hi type="super">23</hi> Who hath enjoined him his way? or who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity? <div eID="gen10156" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10157" type="x-p"/> Elihu here comes more closely to Job; and, <div eID="gen10157" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10158" type="x-p"/> I. He tells him what God would have done for him before this if he had been duly humbled under his affliction. "We all know how ready God is to <hi type="italic">deliver the poor in his affliction</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.36.15">v. 15</reference>); he always was so. The poor in spirit, those that are of a broken and contrite heart, he looks upon with tenderness, and, when they are in affliction, is ready to help them. He <hi type="italic">opens their ears,</hi> and makes them to hear joy and gladness, even <hi type="italic">in</hi> their <hi type="italic">oppressions;</hi> while he does not yet deliver them he speaks to them good words and comfortable words, for the encouragement of their faith and patience, the silencing of their fears, and the balancing of their griefs; and <hi type="italic">even so</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.36.16">v. 16</reference>) would he have done to thee if thou hadst submitted to his providence and conducted thyself well; he would have delivered and comforted thee, and we should have had none of these complaints. If thou hadst accommodated thyself to the will of God, thy liberty and plenty would have been restored to thee with advantage." 1. "Thou wouldst have been enlarged, and not confined thus by thy sickness and disgrace: <hi type="italic">He would have removed thee into a broad place where is no straitness,</hi> and thou wouldst no longer have been cramped thus and have had all thy measures broken." 2. "Thou wouldst have been enriched, and wouldst not have been left in this poor condition; thou wouldst have had thy table richly spread, not only with food convenient, but with the finest of the wheat" (see <reference osisRef="Deut.32.14">Deut. xxxii. 14</reference>) "and the fattest of the flesh." Note, It ought to silence us under our afflictions to consider that, if we were better, it would be every way better with us: if we had answered the ends of an affliction, the affliction would be removed; and deliverance would come if we were ready for it. God would have done well for us if we had conducted ourselves well; <reference osisRef="Ps.81.13-Ps.81.14">Ps. lxxxi. 13, 14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.48.18">Isa. xlviii. 18</reference>. <div eID="gen10158" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10159" type="x-p"/> II. He charges him with standing in his own light, and makes him the cause of the continuance of his own trouble (<reference osisRef="Job.36.17">v. 17</reference>): "<hi type="italic">But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked,</hi>" that is, "Whatever thou art really, in this thing thou hast conducted thyself like a wicked man, hast spoken and done like the wicked, hast gratified them and served their cause; and <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> judgment and justice take hold on thee as a wicked man, because thou goest in company with them, actest as if thou wert in their interest, aiding and abetting. <hi type="italic">Thou hast maintained the cause of the wicked;</hi> and such as a man's cause is such will the judgment of God be upon him;" so bishop Patrick. It is dangerous being on the wrong side: accessaries to treason will be dealt with as principals. <div eID="gen10159" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10160" type="x-p"/> III. He cautions him not to persist in his frowardness. Several good cautions he gives him to this purport. <div eID="gen10160" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10161" type="x-p"/> 1. Let him not make light of divine vengeance, nor be secure, as if he were in no danger of it (<reference osisRef="Job.36.18">v. 18</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Because there is wrath</hi>" (that is, "because God is a righteous governor, who resents all the affronts given to his government, because he has revealed his wrath from heaven against all ungodliness and unrighteousness of men, and because thou hast reason to fear that thou art under God's displeasure) therefore <hi type="italic">beware lest he take thee away</hi> suddenly <hi type="italic">with his stroke,</hi> and be so wise as to make thy peace with him quickly and get his anger turned away from thee." A warning to this purport Job had given his friends (<reference osisRef="Job.19.29">ch. xix. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Be you afraid of the sword, for wrath brings the punishment of the sword.</hi> Thus contenders are apt, with too much boldness, to bind one another over to the judgment of God and threaten one another with his wrath; but he that keeps a good conscience needs not fear the impotent menaces of proud men. But his was a friendly caution to Job, and necessary. Even good men have need to be kept to their duty by the fear of God's wrath. "Thou art a wise and good man, but beware lest he take thee away, for the wisest and best have enough in them to deserve his stroke." <div eID="gen10161" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10162" type="x-p"/> 2. Let him not promise himself that, if God's wrath should kindle against him, he could find out ways to escape the strokes of it. (1.) There is no escaping by money, no purchasing a pardon with silver, or gold, and such corruptible things: "Even <hi type="italic">a great ransom cannot deliver thee</hi> when God enters into judgment with thee. His justice cannot be bribed, nor any of the ministers of his justice. <hi type="italic">Will he esteem thy riches,</hi> and take from them a commutation of the punishment? <hi type="italic">No, not gold,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.19">v. 19</reference>. If thou hadst as much wealth as ever thou hadst, that would not ease thee, would not secure thee from the strokes of God's wrath, in the day of the revelation of which <hi type="italic">riches profit not,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Prov. xi. 4</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Ps.49.7-Ps.49.8">Ps. xlix. 7, 8</reference>. (2.) There is no escaping by rescue: "If <hi type="italic">all the forces of strength</hi> were at thy command, if thou couldst muster ever so many servants and vassals to appear for thee to force thee out of the hands of divine vengeance, it were all in vain; God would not regard it. There is <hi type="italic">none that can deliver out of his hand.</hi>" (3.) There is no escaping by absconding (<reference osisRef="Job.36.20">v. 20</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Desire not the night,</hi> which often favours the retreat of a conquered army and covers it; think not that thou canst so escape the righteous judgment of God, for the <hi type="italic">darkness hideth not from him,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Ps.139.11-Ps.139.12">Ps. cxxxix. 11, 12</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Job.34.22">ch. xxxiv. 22</reference>. "Think not, because in the night people retire to their place, go up to their beds, and it is then easy to escape being discovered by them, that God also ascends to his place, and cannot see thee. No; he <hi type="italic">neither slumbers nor sleeps.</hi> His eyes are open upon the children of men, not only in all places, but at all times. No rocks nor mountains can shelter us from his eye." Some understand it of the night of death; that is the night by which men are <hi type="italic">cut off from their place,</hi> and Job had earnestly breathed for that night, as the hireling desires the evening, <reference osisRef="Job.7.2">ch. vii. 2</reference>. "But do not do so," says Elihu; "for thou knowest not what the night of death is." Those that passionately wish for death, in hopes to make that their shelter from God's wrath, may perhaps be mistaken. There are those whom wrath pursues into that night. <div eID="gen10162" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10163" type="x-p"/> 3. Let him not continue his unjust quarrel with God and his providence, which hitherto he had persisted in when he should have submitted to the affliction (<reference osisRef="Job.36.21">v. 21</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Take heed,</hi> look well to thy own spirit, and <hi type="italic">regard not iniquity,</hi> return not to it (so some), for it is at thy peril if thou do." Let us never dare to think a favourable thought of sin, never indulge it, nor allow ourselves in it. Elihu thinks Job had need of this caution, he having <hi type="italic">chosen iniquity rather than affliction,</hi> that is, having chosen rather to gratify his own pride and humour in contending with God than to mortify it by a submission to him and accepting the punishment. We may take it more generally, and observe that those who choose iniquity rather than affliction make a very foolish choice. Those that ease their cares by sinful pleasures, increase their wealth by sinful pursuits, escape their troubles by sinful projects, and evade sufferings for righteousness' sake by sinful compliances against their consciences, make a choice they will repent of; for there is more evil in the least sin than in the greatest affliction. It is an evil, and only evil. <div eID="gen10163" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10164" type="x-p"/> 4. Let him not dare to prescribe to God, nor give him his measures (<reference osisRef="Job.36.22-Job.36.23">v. 22, 23</reference>): "<hi type="italic">Behold, God exalteth by his power,</hi>" that is, "He does, may, and can set up and pull down whom he pleases, and therefore it is not for thee nor me to contend with him." The more we magnify God the more do we humble and abase ourselves. Now consider, (1.) That God is an absolute sovereign: <hi type="italic">He exalts by his</hi> own <hi type="italic">power,</hi> and not by strength derived from any other. He exalts whom he pleases, exalts those that were afflicted and cast down, by the strength and power which he gives his people; and therefore <hi type="italic">who has enjoined him his way?</hi> Who presides above him in his way? Is there any superior from whom he has his commission and to whom he is accountable? No; he himself is supreme and independent. <hi type="italic">Who puts him in mind of his way?</hi> so some. Does the eternal Mind need a remembrancer? No; his own way, as well as ours, is ever before him. He has not received orders or instructions from any (<reference osisRef="Isa.60.13-Isa.60.14">Isa. lx. 13, 14</reference>), nor is he accountable to any. He enjoins to all the creatures their way; let not us then enjoin him his, but leave it to him to govern the world, who is fit to do it. (2.) That he is an incomparable teacher: <hi type="italic">Who teaches like him?</hi> It is absurd for us to teach him who is himself the fountain of light, truth, knowledge, and instruction. <hi type="italic">He that teaches man knowledge,</hi> and so as none else can, <hi type="italic">shall not he know?</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.94.9-Ps.94.10">Ps. xciv. 9, 10</reference>. Shall we light a candle to the sun? Observe, When Elihu would give glory to God as a ruler he praises him as a teacher, for rulers must teach. God does so. He binds with the cords of a man. In this, as in other things, he is unequalled. None so fit to direct his own actions as he himself is. He knows what he has to do, and how to do it for the best, and needs no information nor advice. Solomon himself had a privy-council to advise him, but the King of kings has none. Nor is any so fit to direct our actions as he is. None teaches with such authority and convincing evidence, with such condescension and compassion, nor with such power and efficacy, as God does. He teaches by the Bible, and that is the best book, teaches by his Son, and he is the best Master. (3.) That he is unexceptionably just in all his proceedings: <hi type="italic">Who can say, Thou hast wrought iniquity?</hi> Not, Who <hi type="italic">dares</hi> say it? (many do iniquity, and those who tell them of it do so at their peril), but Who <hi type="italic">can</hi> say it? Who has any cause to say it? Who can say it and prove it? It is a maxim undoubtedly true, without limitation, that <hi type="italic">the King of kings can do no wrong.</hi>
entries.234d718ce8a7ff2808eda634751b86a41373f4bc: <div eID="gen10164" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10165" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">24</hi> Remember that thou magnify his work, which men behold. <hi type="super">25</hi> Every man may see it; man may behold <hi type="italic">it</hi> afar off. <hi type="super">26</hi> Behold, God <hi type="italic">is</hi> great, and we know <hi type="italic">him</hi> not, neither can the number of his years be searched out. <hi type="super">27</hi> For he maketh small the drops of water: they pour down rain according to the vapour thereof: <hi type="super">28</hi> Which the clouds do drop <hi type="italic">and</hi> distil upon man abundantly. 29 Also can <hi type="italic">any</hi> understand the spreadings of the clouds, <hi type="italic">or</hi> the noise of his tabernacle? <hi type="super">30</hi> Behold, he spreadeth his light upon it, and covereth the bottom of the sea. 31 For by them judgeth he the people; he giveth meat in abundance. <hi type="super">32</hi> With clouds he covereth the light; and commandeth it <hi type="italic">not to shine</hi> by <hi type="italic">the cloud</hi> that cometh betwixt. <hi type="super">33</hi> The noise thereof showeth concerning it, the cattle also concerning the vapour. <div eID="gen10165" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10166" type="x-p"/> Elihu is here endeavouring to possess Job with great and high thoughts of God, and so to persuade him into a cheerful submission to his providence. <div eID="gen10166" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10167" type="x-p"/> I. He represents the work of God, in general, as illustrious and conspicuous, <reference osisRef="Job.36.24">v. 24</reference>. His whole work is so. God does nothing mean. This is a good reason why we should acquiesce in all the operations of his providence concerning us in particular. His visible works, those of nature, and which concern the world in general, are such as we admire and commend, and in which we observe the Creator's wisdom, power, and goodness; shall we then find fault with his dispensations concerning us, and the counsels of his will concerning our affairs? We are here called to <hi type="italic">consider the work of God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.13">Eccl. vii. 13</reference>. 1. It is plain before our eyes, nothing more obvious: it is what <hi type="italic">men behold.</hi> Every man that has but half an eye may see it, may behold it afar off. Look which way we will, we see the productions of God's wisdom and power; we see that done, and that doing, concerning which we cannot but say, This is <hi type="italic">the work of God,</hi> the finger of God; it is the Lord's doing. Every man may see, afar off, the heaven and all its lights, the earth and all its fruits, to be the work of Omnipotence; much more when we behold them nigh at hand. Look at the minutest works of nature through a microscope; do they not appear curious? The eternal power and godhead of the Creator are <hi type="italic">clearly seen and understood</hi> by the <hi type="italic">things that are made,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rom.1.20">Rom. i. 20</reference>. Every man, even those that have not the benefit of divine revelation, may see this; for <hi type="italic">there is no speech or language where the voice</hi> of these natural constant preachers <hi type="italic">is not heard,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.19.3">Ps. xix. 3</reference>. 2. It ought to be marvellous in our eyes. The beauty and excellency of the work of God, and the agreement of all the parts of it, are what we must remember to magnify and highly to extol, not only justify it as right and good, and what cannot be blamed, but magnify it as wise and glorious, and such as no creature could contrive or produce. Man may see his works, and is capable of discerning his hand in them (which the beasts are not), and therefore ought to praise them and give him the glory of them. <div eID="gen10167" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10168" type="x-p"/> II. He represents God, the author of them, as infinite and unsearchable, <reference osisRef="Job.36.26">v. 26</reference>. The streams of being, power, and perfection should lead us to the fountain. <hi type="italic">God is great,</hi> infinitely so,—great in power, for he is omnipotent and independent,—great in wealth, for he is self-sufficient and all-sufficient,—great in himself,—great in all his works,—great, and therefore greatly to be praised,—great, and therefore <hi type="italic">we know him not.</hi> We know that he is, but not what he is. We know what he is not, but not what he is. We know in part, but not in perfection. This comes in here as a reason why we must not arraign his proceedings, nor find fault with what he does, because it is speaking evil of the things that we understand not and answering a matter before we hear if. We know not the duration of his existence, for it is infinite. <hi type="italic">The number of his years cannot</hi> possibly <hi type="italic">be searched out,</hi> for he is eternal; there is no number of them. He is a Being without beginning, succession, or period, whoever was, and ever will be, and ever the same, the great <hi type="italic">I AM.</hi> This is a good reason why we should not prescribe to him, nor quarrel with him, because, as he is, such are his operations, quite out of our reach. <div eID="gen10168" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10169" type="x-p"/> III. He gives some instances of God's wisdom, power, and sovereign dominion, in the works of nature and the dispensations of common providence, beginning in this chapter with the clouds and the rain that descends from them. We need not be critical in examining either the phrase or the philosophy of this noble discourse. The general scope of it is to show that God is infinitely great, and the Lord of all, the first cause and supreme director of all the creatures, and <hi type="italic">has all power in heaven and earth</hi> (whom therefore we ought, with all humility and reverence, to adore, to speak well of, and to give honour to), and that it is presumption for us to prescribe to him the rules and methods of his special providence towards the children of men, or to expect from him an account of them, when the operations even of common providences about the meteors are so various and so mysterious and unaccountable. Elihu, to affect Job with God's sublimity and sovereignty, had directed him (<reference osisRef="Job.35.5">ch. xxxv. 5</reference>) to look unto the clouds. In <reference osisRef="Job.36.24-Job.36.33">these verses</reference> he shows us what we may observe in the clouds we see which will lead us to consider the glorious perfections of their Creator. Consider the clouds, <div eID="gen10169" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10170" type="x-p"/> 1. As springs to this lower world, the source and treasure of its moisture, and the great bank through which it circulates—a very necessary provision, for its stagnation would be as hurtful to this lower world as that of the blood to the body of man. It is worth while to observe in this common occurrence, (1.) That the clouds above distil upon the earth below. If the heavens become brass, the earth becomes iron; therefore thus the promise of plenty runs, <hi type="italic">I will hear the heavens and they shall hear the earth.</hi> This intimates to us that every good gift is from above, from him who is both Father of lights and Father of the rain, and it instructs us to direct our prayers to him and to look up. (2.) That they are here said to <hi type="italic">distil upon man</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.36.28">v. 28</reference>); for, though indeed God <hi type="italic">causes it to rain in the wilderness where no man is</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.38.26">ch. xxxviii. 26</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.104.11">Ps. civ. 11</reference>), yet special respect is had to man herein, to whom the inferior creatures are all made serviceable and from whom the actual return of the tribute of praise is required. Among men, he <hi type="italic">causes his rain to fall upon the just and upon the unjust,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.5.45">Matt. v. 45</reference>. (3.) They are said to distil the water in <hi type="italic">small drops,</hi> not in spouts, as when the <hi type="italic">windows of heaven were opened,</hi> <reference osisRef="Gen.7.11">Gen. vii. 11</reference>. God waters the earth with that with which he once drowned it, only dispensing it in another manner, to let us know how much we lie at his mercy, and how kind he is, in giving rain by drops, that the benefit of it may be the further and the more equally diffused, as by an artificial water-pot. (4.) Though sometimes the rain comes in very small drops, yet, at other times, it pours down in great rain, and this difference between one shower and another must be resolved into the divine Providence which orders it so. (5.) Though it comes down in drops, yet it distils upon man <hi type="italic">abundantly</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.36.28">v. 28</reference>), and therefore is called <hi type="italic">the river of God which is full of water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.9">Ps. lxv. 9</reference>. (6.) The clouds <hi type="italic">pour down according to the vapour</hi> that they draw up, <reference osisRef="Job.36.27">v. 27</reference>. So just the heavens are to the earth, but the earth is not so in the return it makes. (7.) The produce of the clouds is sometimes a great terror, and at other times a great favour, to the earth, <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">v. 31</reference>. When he pleases <hi type="italic">by them he judges the people</hi> he is angry with. Storms, and tempests, and excessive rains, destroying the fruits of the earth and causing inundations, come from the clouds; but, on the other hand, from them, usually, he gives meat in abundance; they drop fatness upon the pastures that are clothed with flocks, and the valleys that are <hi type="italic">covered with corn,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.65.11-Ps.65.13">Ps. lxv. 11-13</reference>. (8.) Notice is sometimes given of the approach of rain, <reference osisRef="Job.36.33">v. 33</reference>. <hi type="italic">The noise thereof,</hi> among other things, <hi type="italic">shows concerning it.</hi> Hence we read (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.18.41">1 Kings xviii. 41</reference>) of <hi type="italic">the sound of abundance of rain,</hi> or (as it is in the margin) <hi type="italic">a sound of a noise of rain,</hi> before it came; and a welcome harbinger it was then. As the noise, so the face of the sky, shows concerning it, <reference osisRef="Luke.12.56">Luke xii. 56</reference>. The cattle also, by a strange instinct, are apprehensive of a change in the weather nigh at hand, and seek for shelter, shaming man, who will not foresee the evil and hide himself. <div eID="gen10170" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen10171" type="x-p"/> 2. As shadows to the upper world (<reference osisRef="Job.36.29">v. 29</reference>): <hi type="italic">Can any understand the spreading of the clouds?</hi> They are spread over the earth as a curtain or canopy; how they come to be so, how stretched out, and how poised, as they are, we cannot understand, though we daily see they are so. Shall we then pretend to understand the reasons and methods of God's judicial proceedings with the children of men, whose characters and cases are so various, when we cannot account for the spreadings of the clouds, which <hi type="italic">cover the light?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">v. 32</reference>. It is a cloud coming <hi type="italic">betwixt,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">v. 32</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.26.9">ch. xxvi. 9</reference>. And this we are sensible of, that, by the interposition of the clouds between us and the sun, we are, (1.) Sometimes favoured; for they serve as an umbrella to shelter us from the violent heat of the sun, which otherwise would beat upon us. A <hi type="italic">cloud of dew in the heat of harvest</hi> is spoken of as a very great refreshment. <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Isa. xviii. 4</reference>. (2.) Sometimes we are by them frowned upon; for they darken the earth at noon-day and eclipse the light of the sun. Sin is compared to a cloud (<reference osisRef="Isa.44.22">Isa. xliv. 22</reference>), because it comes between us and the light of God's countenance and obstructs the shining of it. But though the clouds darken the sun for a time, and pour down rain, yet (<hi type="italic">post nubila Phoebus</hi>—<hi type="italic">the sun shines forth after the rain</hi>), after he has wearied the cloud, <hi type="italic">he spreads his light upon it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.36.30">v. 30</reference>. There is a <hi type="italic">clear shining after rain,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Sam.23.4">2 Sam. xxiii. 4</reference>. The sunbeams are darted forth, and reach to <hi type="italic">cover</hi> even <hi type="italic">the bottom of the sea,</hi> thence to exhale a fresh supply of vapours, and so raise recruits for the clouds, <reference osisRef="Job.36.30">v. 30</reference>. In all this, we must remember to magnify the work of God.  <chapter eID="Job.36"/> <div eID="gen10171" type="x-p"/>

entries.4e11eaf7787f42305134d889b63a1bf3433ad63b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5259"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 36</title> <div sID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Job.36.1-Job.36.33">Job 36:1-33</reference>.<div eID="gen7847" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7848" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5259"/>1-2. Elihu maintains that afflictions are to the godly disciplinary, in order to lead them to attain a higher moral worth, and that the reason for their continuance is not, as the friends asserted, on account of the sufferer's extraordinary guilt, but because the discipline has not yet attained its object, namely, to lend him to humble himself penitently before God (<reference osisRef="Isa.9.13">Is 9:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.5.3">Jr 5:3</reference>). This is Elihu's fourth speech. He thus exceeds the ternary number of the others. Hence his formula of politeness (<reference osisRef="Job.36.2">Job 36:2</reference>). Literally, "Wait yet but a little for me." Bear with me a little farther. I have yet (much, <reference osisRef="Job.32.18-Job.32.20">Job 32:18-20</reference>). There are Chaldeisms in this verse, agreeably to the view that the scene of the book is near the Euphrates and the Chaldees. <div eID="gen7848" type="x-p"/>
entries.81f258a7ff2f5e42ae8acee184f705b4bc11079e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5260"/><div sID="gen7849" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5260"/><hi type="bold">3. from afar--</hi>not trite commonplaces, but drawn from God's mighty works.<div eID="gen7849" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7850" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ascribe righteousness--</hi>whereas Job ascribed unrighteousness (<reference osisRef="Job.34.10">Job 34:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.12">12</reference>). A man, in enquiring into God's ways, should at the outset presume they are all just, be willing to find them so, and expect that the result of investigation will prove them to be so; such a one will never be disappointed [Barnes]. <div eID="gen7850" type="x-p"/>
entries.7517fb04f6a1f6e161f2ac6d71a02ba13aace0d3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5261"/><div sID="gen7851" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5261"/><hi type="bold">4. I will not "speak wickedly for God," as the friends (<reference osisRef="Job.13.4">Job 13:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.7.8">7, 8</reference>)--</hi>that is, vindicate God by unsound arguments.<div eID="gen7851" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7852" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">he that is perfect, &c.--</hi>Rather, as the parallelism requires, "a man of integrity in sentiments is with thee" (is he with whom thou hast to do). Elihu means himself, as opposed to the dishonest reasonings of the friends (<reference osisRef="Job.21.34">Job 21:34</reference>). <div eID="gen7852" type="x-p"/>
entries.02f6ccf20892bdb0b697d07f5c49fe3510ff32b2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5262"/><div sID="gen7853" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5262"/>5. Rather, "strength of understanding" (heart) the force of the repetition of "mighty"; as "mighty" as God is, none is too low to be "despised" by Him; for His "might" lies especially in "His strength of understanding," whereby He searches out the most minute things, so as to give to each his right. Elihu confirms his exhortation (<reference osisRef="Job.35.14">Job 35:14</reference>). <div eID="gen7853" type="x-p"/>
entries.0f248053f40faed0e45a65c022125554b2733465: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5263"/><div sID="gen7854" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5263"/><hi type="bold">6. right ... poor--</hi>He espouses the cause of the afflicted. <div eID="gen7854" type="x-p"/>
entries.74b22bb592140c30ab1536105786cd03092d4d52: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5264"/><div sID="gen7855" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5264"/>7. (<reference osisRef="1Pet.3.12">1Pe 3:12</reference>). God does not forsake the godly, as Job implied, but "establishes," or makes them sit on the throne as kings (<reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7">Psa 113:7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.8">8</reference>). True of believers in the highest sense, already in part (<reference osisRef="1Pet.2.9">1Pe 2:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Re 1:6</reference>); hereafter fully (<reference osisRef="Rev.5.10">Re 5:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.22.5">Job 22:5</reference>).<div eID="gen7855" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7856" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and they are--</hi>that they may be. <div eID="gen7856" type="x-p"/>
entries.d5576659fb1f996a2f3e91c2579643a79ad853cd: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5265"/><div sID="gen7857" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5265"/>8-10. If they be afflicted, it is no proof that they are hypocrites, as the friends maintain, or that God disregards them, and is indifferent whether men are good or bad, as Job asserts: God is thereby "disciplining them," and "showing them their sins," and if they bow in a right spirit under God's visiting hand, the greatest blessings ensue. <div eID="gen7857" type="x-p"/>
entries.1bde03b34d60f60af2037fa5d8b081214cf8e611: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5268"/><div sID="gen7861" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5268"/><hi type="bold">11. serve--</hi>that is, worship; as in <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23">Is 19:23</reference>. God is to be supplied (compare <reference osisRef="Isa.1.19">Is 1:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.1.20">20</reference>). <div eID="gen7861" type="x-p"/>
entries.f14964d9ce19cffae0a04f8255d93a7232b3b3b3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5269"/><div sID="gen7862" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5269"/>12. (<reference osisRef="Job.33.18">Job 33:18</reference>).<div eID="gen7862" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7863" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">without knowledge--</hi>that is, on account of their foolishness (<reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.4.21">21</reference>). <div eID="gen7863" type="x-p"/>
entries.37d00e20997359ef75014d1c1e9a4564e0f221c4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5270"/><div sID="gen7864" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5270"/>13-15. Same sentiment as <reference osisRef="Job.36.11">Job 36:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.12">12</reference>, expanded.<div eID="gen7864" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7865" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hypocrites--</hi>or, the ungodly [Maurer]; but "hypocrites" is perhaps a distinct class from the openly wicked (<reference osisRef="Job.36.12">Job 36:12</reference>).<div eID="gen7865" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7866" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">heap up wrath--</hi>of God against themselves (<reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Ro 2:5</reference>). Umbreit translates, "nourish their wrath against God," instead of "crying" unto Him. This suits well the parallelism and the Hebrew. But the English Version gives a good parallelism, "hypocrites" answering to "cry not" (<reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job 27:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.27.10">10</reference>); "heap up wrath" against themselves, to "He bindeth them" with fetters of affliction (<reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference>). <div eID="gen7866" type="x-p"/>
entries.40c74f471b4b44b14d726d4d83f5b5e9965d0f36: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5273"/><div sID="gen7870" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5273"/>16. Rather, "He will lead forth thee also out of the jaws of a strait" (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.19">Psa 18:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.118.5">118:5</reference>).<div eID="gen7870" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7871" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">broad place--</hi>expresses the liberty, and the well-supplied "table" the abundance of the prosperous (<reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.25.6">Is 25:6</reference>). <div eID="gen7871" type="x-p"/>
entries.f24ae90e1351382cba435a5729c0e098cc356afe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5274"/><div sID="gen7872" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5274"/>17. Rather, "But if thou art fulfilled (that is, entirely filled) with the judgment of the wicked (that is, the guilt incurring judgment" [Maurer]; or rather, as Umbreit, referring to Job 34:5-7, 36, the judgment pronounced on God by the guilty in misfortunes), judgment (God's judgment on the wicked, <reference osisRef="Jer.51.9">Jr 51:9</reference>, playing on the double meaning of "judgment") and justice shall closely follow each other [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7872" type="x-p"/>
entries.e8f29df90733ee83aee556f6d5e964dd59d688ad: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5275"/><div sID="gen7873" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5275"/>18. (<reference osisRef="Num.16.45">Nu 16:45</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.49.6">Psa 49:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.49.7">7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.16.26">Mt 16:26</reference>). Even the "ransom" by Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Job.33.24">Job 33:24</reference>) will be of no avail to wilful despisers (<reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29">He 10:26-29</reference>).<div eID="gen7873" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7874" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">with his stroke--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Job.34.26">Job 34:26</reference>). Umbreit translates, "Beware lest the wrath of God (thy severe calamity) lead thee to scorn" (<reference osisRef="Job.34.7">Job 34:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">27:23</reference>). This accords better with the verb in the parallel clause, which ought to be translated, "Let not the great ransom (of money, which thou canst give) seduce thee (Margin, turn thee aside, as if thou couldst deliver thyself from "wrath" by it). As the "scorn" in the first clause answers to the "judgment of the wicked" (<reference osisRef="Job.36.17">Job 36:17</reference>), so "ransom" ("seduce") to "will he esteem riches" (<reference osisRef="Job.36.19">Job 36:19</reference>). Thus, <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference> is the transition between <reference osisRef="Job.36.17">Job 36:17</reference> and <reference osisRef="Job.36.19">Job 36:19</reference>. <div eID="gen7874" type="x-p"/>
entries.ea43282f6f0dcd4e81f620be18d8572632dacac2: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5276"/><div sID="gen7875" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5276"/><hi type="bold">19. forces of strength--</hi>that is, resources of wealth (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.7">Psa 49:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.11.4">Pr 11:4</reference>). <div eID="gen7875" type="x-p"/>
entries.a80028015ca98f21f316a9519b213945e4a81a6b: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5277"/><div sID="gen7876" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5277"/><hi type="bold">20. Desire--</hi>pant for. Job had wished for death (<reference osisRef="Job.3.3-Job.3.9">Job 3:3-9</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen7876" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7877" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">night--</hi>(<reference osisRef="John.9.4">Joh 9:4</reference>).<div eID="gen7877" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7878" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">when--</hi>rather, "whereby."<div eID="gen7878" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7879" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">cut off--</hi>literally, "ascend," as the corn cut and lifted upon the wagon or stack (<reference osisRef="Job.36.26">Job 36:26</reference>); so "cut off," "disappear."<div eID="gen7879" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7880" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in their place--</hi>literally, "under themselves"; so, without moving from their place, on the spot, suddenly (<reference osisRef="Job.40.12">Job 40:12</reference>) [Maurer]. Umbreit's translation: "To ascend (which is really, as thou wilt find to thy cost, to descend) to the people below" (literally, "under themselves"), answers better to the parallelism and the Hebrew. Thou pantest for death as desirable, but it is a "night" or region of darkness; thy fancied ascent (amelioration) will prove a descent (deterioration) (<reference osisRef="Job.10.22">Job 10:22</reference>); therefore desire it not. <div eID="gen7880" type="x-p"/>
entries.e445245ff06ce38503836e021c3b3a3ff869fbd0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5278"/><div sID="gen7881" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5278"/><hi type="bold">21. regard--</hi>literally, "turn thyself to."<div eID="gen7881" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7882" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">iniquity--</hi>namely, presumptuous speaking against God (<reference osisRef="Job.34.5">Job 34:5</reference>, and above, see on <reference osisRef="Job.36.17">Job 36:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">18</reference>).<div eID="gen7882" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7883" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">rather than--</hi>to bear "affliction" with pious patience. Men think it an alleviation to complain against God, but this is adding sin to sorrow; it is sin, not sorrow, which can really hurt us (contrast <reference osisRef="Heb.11.25">He 11:25</reference>). <div eID="gen7883" type="x-p"/>
entries.f59bc6717acdfd82b473adaf39094c156fcf08cf: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5279"/><div sID="gen7884" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5279"/>22-25. God is not to be impiously arraigned, but to be praised for His might, shown in His works.<div eID="gen7884" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7885" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">exalteth--</hi>rather, doeth lofty things, shows His exalted power [Umbreit] (<reference osisRef="Ps.21.13">Psa 21:13</reference>).<div eID="gen7885" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7886" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">teacheth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.94.12">Psa 94:12</reference>, &c.). The connection is, returning to <reference osisRef="Job.36.5">Job 36:5</reference>, God's "might" is shown in His "wisdom"; He alone can teach; yet, because He, as a sovereign, explains not all His dealings, forsooth Job must presume to teach Him (<reference osisRef="Isa.40.13">Is 40:13</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.40.14">14</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.11.34">Ro 11:34</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.2.16">1Co 2:16</reference>). So the transition to <reference osisRef="Job.36.23">Job 36:23</reference> is natural. Umbreit with the Septuagint translates, "Who is Lord," wrongly, as this meaning belongs to later Hebrew. <div eID="gen7886" type="x-p"/>
entries.b28ea1cfb11ea4cf1c238264452b7c8954a1e878: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5283"/><div sID="gen7892" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5283"/>26. (<reference osisRef="Job.37.13">Job 37:13</reference>). God's greatness in heaven and earth: a reason why Job should bow under His afflicting hand.<div eID="gen7892" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7893" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">know him not--</hi>only in part (<reference osisRef="Job.36.25">Job 36:25</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Cor.13.12">1Co 13:12</reference>).<div eID="gen7893" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7894" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">his years--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Ps.90.2">Psa 90:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.102.24">102:24</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.102.27">27</reference>); applied to Jesus Christ (<reference osisRef="Heb.1.12">He 1:12</reference>). <div eID="gen7894" type="x-p"/>
entries.4830733aba8fde36d170ebe56e82bf48a3a8ed21: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5284"/><div sID="gen7895" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5284"/>27-28. The marvellous formation of rain (so <reference osisRef="Job.5.9">Job 5:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.5.10">10</reference>).<div eID="gen7895" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7896" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">maketh small--</hi>Rather, "He draweth (up) to Him, He attracts (from the earth below) the drops of water; they (the drops of water) pour down rain, (which is) His vapor." "Vapor" is in apposition with "rain," marking the way in which rain is formed; namely, from the vapor drawn up by God into the air and then condensed into drops, which fall (<reference osisRef="Ps.147.8">Psa 147:8</reference>). The suspension of such a mass of water, and its descent not in a deluge, but in drops of vapory rain, are the marvel. The selection of this particular illustration of God's greatness forms a fit prelude to the storm in which God appears (<reference osisRef="Job.40.1">Job 40:1</reference>). <div eID="gen7896" type="x-p"/>
entries.6af7ed658bab04ff54a64090ed2a4feb1dafc73d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5286"/><div sID="gen7898" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5286"/>29. (<reference osisRef="Job.37.5">Job 37:5</reference>). God's marvels in thunder and lightnings.<div eID="gen7898" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7899" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spreadings, &c.--</hi>the canopy of thick clouds, which covers the heavens in a storm (<reference osisRef="Ps.105.39">Psa 105:39</reference>).<div eID="gen7899" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7900" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the noise--</hi>"crashing"; namely, thunder.<div eID="gen7900" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7901" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of his tabernacle--</hi>God being poetically said to have His pavilion amid dark clouds (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.11">Psa 18:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.40.22">Is 40:22</reference>). <div eID="gen7901" type="x-p"/>
entries.dc0b3d2ec07c9a8e7de6bc8611be470b7b9f8bdc: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5287"/><div sID="gen7902" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5287"/><hi type="bold">30. light--</hi>lightning.<div eID="gen7902" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7903" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">it--</hi>His tabernacle (<reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference>). The light, in an instant spread over the vast mass of dark clouds, forms a striking picture.<div eID="gen7903" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7904" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">spread--</hi>is repeated from <reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference> to form an antithesis. "He spreads not only clouds, but light."<div eID="gen7904" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7905" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">covereth the bottom--</hi>roots.<div eID="gen7905" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen7906" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">of the sea--</hi>namely, with the light. In the storm the depths of ocean are laid bare; and the light "covers" them, at the same moment that it "spreads" across the dark sky. So in <reference osisRef="Ps.18.14">Psa 18:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.18.15">15</reference>, the discovering of "the channels of waters" follows the "lightnings." Umbreit translates: "He spreadeth His light upon Himself, and covereth Himself with the roots of the sea" (<reference osisRef="Ps.104.2">Psa 104:2</reference>). God's garment is woven of celestial light and of the watery depths, raised to the sky to form His cloudy canopy. The phrase, "cover Himself with the roots of the sea," is harsh; but the image is grand. <div eID="gen7906" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6c481141fad1742d7494bc432a89a81f973e9c3: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5288"/><div sID="gen7907" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5288"/>31. These (rain and lightnings) are marvellous and not to be understood (<reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference>), yet necessary. "For by them He judgeth (chastiseth on the one hand), &c. (and on the other, by them) He giveth meat" (food), &c. (<reference osisRef="Job.37.13">Job 37:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.38.23">38:23</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.38.27">27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Acts.14.17">Ac 14:17</reference>). <div eID="gen7907" type="x-p"/>
entries.82fbe200f074ecd968f9bad3af91e93f22886de4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5289"/><div sID="gen7908" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5289"/>32. Rather, "He covereth (both) His hands with light (lightning, <reference osisRef="Job.37.3">Job 37:3</reference>, Margin), and giveth it a command against his adversary" (literally, the one "assailing" Him, <reference osisRef="Ps.8.2">Psa 8:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.139.20">139:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.21.19">Job 21:19</reference>). Thus, as in <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference>, the twofold effects of His waters are set forth, so here, of His light; in the one hand, destructive lightning against the wicked; in the other, the genial light for good to His friends, &c. (<reference osisRef="Job.36.33">Job 36:33</reference>) [Umbreit]. <div eID="gen7908" type="x-p"/>
entries.af4685493fb0fd89a4a94c0efe28cd5d13c8e55e: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv5290"/><div sID="gen7909" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv5290"/><hi type="bold">33. noise--</hi>rather, He revealeth it (literally, "announceth concerning it") to His friend (antithesis to adversary, <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">Job 36:32</reference>, so the Hebrew is translated, <reference osisRef="Job.2.11">Job 2:11</reference>); also to cattle and plants (literally, "that which shooteth up"; <reference osisRef="Gen.40.10">Ge 40:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="Gen.41.22">41:22</reference>). As the genial effect of "water" in the growth of food, is mentioned, <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference>, so here that of "light" in cherishing cattle and plants [Umbreit]. If English Version, "noise" be retained, translate, "His noise (thunder) announces concerning Him (His coming in the tempest), the cattle (to announce) concerning Him when He is in the act of rising up" (in the storm). Some animals give various intimations that they are sensible of the approach of a storm [Virgil, Georgics, I.373, &c.]. <chapter eID="Job.36"/>

entries.6ea8c74c9d6edb3b3d925cb02d1b1101f15351b6: <div eID="gen17705" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s">Introduction</title> <div sID="gen17706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17707" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen17706" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen17708" type="x-p"/> Elihu vindicates God's justice, and his providential and gracious dealings with men, <reference osisRef="Job.36.1-Job.36.9">Job 36:1-9</reference>. Promises of God to the obedient, and threatenings to the disobedient; also promises to the poor and afflicted, <reference osisRef="Job.36.10-Job.36.16">Job 36:10-16</reference>. Sundry proofs of God's merely, with suitable exhortations and cautions, vv. 17-33. <div eID="gen17708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17709" type="x-p"/> <hi type="bold">Verse 1</hi> <div eID="gen17709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17710" type="x-p"/> Elihu also proceeded - Mr. Heath gives a good summary of this chapter. Elihu goes on to lay before Job the impropriety of his behavior towards God, and desires him to consider how vain it will prove. That God Almighty will never yield the point; that he will administer impartial justice to all men, <reference osisRef="Job.36.2-Job.36.6">Job 36:2-6</reference>. That the general course of his providence is to favor the righteous: and that though he may sometimes correct them in love, yet if they submit patiently to his fatherly corrections, they shall enjoy all manner of prosperity; but if they be stubborn, and will not submit, they will only draw down greater proofs of his displeasure, <reference osisRef="Job.36.7-Job.36.16">Job 36:7-16</reference>. He tells him that, had he followed the former course, he had probably, before now, been restored to his former condition; whereas, by persisting in the latter course, he was in a fair way of becoming a signal example of Divine justice, <reference osisRef="Job.36.17">Job 36:17</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference>. He therefore warns him to use the present opportunity, lest God should cut him off while he was in a state of rebellion against him; for with God neither wealth, power, nor any other argument that he could use, would be of any avail, <reference osisRef="Job.36.18-Job.36.26">Job 36:18-26</reference>. That God was infinitely powerful; there was no resisting him: and infinitely wise, as sufficiently appeared by his works; there was, therefore, no escaping out of his hands. That his purity was so great that the sun, in his presence, was more dim than the smallest ray of light when compared to that grand luminary; that his holiness was manifest by his aversion to iniquity; and his goodness, in supplying the wants of his creatures.
entries.4bf3a6dcccf6f162d883875ffa2623f8b6960bcf: <hi type="bold">Verse 2</hi> <div eID="gen17710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17711" type="x-p"/> That I have yet to speak on God's behalf - I have other proofs to allege in behalf of God's justice and providence.
entries.a926409c39c058faa4392238dba6cd19f99e22c6: <hi type="bold">Verse 3</hi> <div eID="gen17711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17712" type="x-p"/> I will fetch my knowledge from afar - למרחוק lemerachok, "from the distant place," meaning probably both remote antiquity and heaven; see below. I will show thee that all antiquity and experience are on my side. I can bring proofs from the remotest ages and from the most distant countries to demonstrate that God is infinitely Wise, and can do nothing foolish or erroneous; that he is infinitely Powerful, and can bring all the purposes of his wisdom to effect; that he is infinitely Good, and can will nothing, and can do nothing that is not good in itself, and well calculated to do good to his creatures. And I shall show that his operations in the heavens and on the earth prove and demonstrate the whole. <div eID="gen17712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17713" type="x-p"/> And will ascribe righteousness to my Maker - By proving the above points, the righteous conduct of God, and his gracious government of the world, will be fully established. That Elihu brings his knowledge from afar - from every part of the creation, as well as from the Divine nature - is evident from the end of the chapter. <div eID="gen17713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17714" type="x-p"/> 1. The omnipotence of God; - God is great. <div eID="gen17714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17715" type="x-p"/> 2. The eternity of God - We know him not, the number of his years cannot be found out, <reference osisRef="Job.36.26">Job 36:26</reference>. <div eID="gen17715" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17716" type="x-p"/> 3. From the economy of God in the atmosphere, in dews, rain, vapor, and the irrigation of the earth; - He maketh small the drops, etc., <reference osisRef="Job.36.27">Job 36:27</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.28">Job 36:28</reference>. <div eID="gen17716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17717" type="x-p"/> 4. In the thunder and lightning, by which he performs such wonders in the atmosphere, and executes such judgments in the world; - Also who can understand the noise of his tabernacle? He spreadeth his light upon it. He judgeth the people, etc., <reference osisRef="Job.36.29-Job.36.33">Job 36:29-33</reference>.
entries.c9acb2105ac00d8da8712909bcec935fed441b56: <hi type="bold">Verse 4</hi> <div eID="gen17717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17718" type="x-p"/> My words shall not be false - My words shall be truth without falsity. <div eID="gen17718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17719" type="x-p"/> He that is perfect in knowledge is with thee - "The perfection of knowledge is with thee." Thou art a sensible, well-informed man, and will be able to judge of what I say.
entries.f186c228e70810b5adb22d0ea7206ddef98a9d4f: <hi type="bold">Verse 5</hi> <div eID="gen17719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17720" type="x-p"/> God is mighty and despiseth not any - He reproaches no man for his want of knowledge. If any man lack wisdom, he may come to God, who giveth liberally, and upbraideth not. I prefer this to the passive sense, will not be despised. <div eID="gen17720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17721" type="x-p"/> He is mighty - Literally, "He is mighty in strength of heart;" he can never be terrified nor alarmed.
entries.c27db1c6e6759b923c945e5e49b5ff9c8b69bfc3: <hi type="bold">Verse 6</hi> <div eID="gen17721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17722" type="x-p"/> He preserveth not the life - He will not give life to the wicked; all such forfeit life by their transgressions. <div eID="gen17722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17723" type="x-p"/> But giveth right - Justice will he give to the afflicted or humble, עניים aniyim.
entries.4d9d7847602d315ace22a971cb01f9f64790b9df: <hi type="bold">Verse 7</hi> <div eID="gen17723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17724" type="x-p"/> He withdraweth not his eyes - Exactly similar to those words of David, <reference osisRef="Psa.34.15">Psa 34:15</reference> : "The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous." <div eID="gen17724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17725" type="x-p"/> But with kings are they on the throne - I think the words should be read thus: - "But with kings upon the throne shall he place them; and they shall be exalted for ever." The word וישיבם vaiyeshibem, he will establish or place them, should be added to the first clause, as I have done; and then the sense becomes much clearer. Instead of לנצח fo da lanetsach, forever, perhaps to victory would be a better sense: "But with kings upon the throne will he place them; and they shall be exalted or triumph to victory." This is precisely the same idea, and conveyed in nearly the same words, as that of our Lord: - "To him that overcometh will I grant to sit with me in my throne, even as I also overcame, and am set down with my Father in his throne;" <reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev 3:21</reference>. "Unto him that loved us, and washed us from our sins in his own blood, and hath made us kings and priests unto God and his Father, to him be glory," etc.; <reference osisRef="Rev.1.5">Rev 1:5</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.1.6">Rev 1:6</reference>.
entries.63c5e4a65957a692e6dc201258a8d098bd5e4704: <hi type="bold">Verse 8</hi> <div eID="gen17725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17726" type="x-p"/> And if they be bound in fetters - These are means which God uses, not of punishment, but of correction.
entries.1696ba0d09873ab2db8e24b428aa54628fb5f5f1: <hi type="bold">Verse 9</hi> <div eID="gen17726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17727" type="x-p"/> He showeth them their work - He shows them the exceeding sinfulness of sin. <div eID="gen17727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17728" type="x-p"/> That they have exceeded - יתגברו yithgabbaru, "that they have strengthened themselves," and did not trust in the living God; and therefore they would not help themselves when trouble came.
entries.3172be982ae9d5d19f5fe009b33361d731628d86: <hi type="bold">Verse 10</hi> <div eID="gen17728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17729" type="x-p"/> He openeth also their ear - He gives them to understand the reason why they are thus corrected, and commands them to return from those iniquities which have induced him to visit them with afflictions and distresses.
entries.4787c42a1eb6a9990f5540545c40b40fa939af9b: <hi type="bold">Verse 11</hi> <div eID="gen17729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17730" type="x-p"/> If they obey and serve him - There may appear in the course of Providence to be some exceptions to this general rule; but it is most true, that this is literally or spiritually fulfilled to all the genuine followers of God. Every man is happy, in whatsoever circumstances, whose heart is unreservedly dedicated to his Maker.
entries.afaf18cca88cefbf8c10400035a657bc0e153201: <hi type="bold">Verse 12</hi> <div eID="gen17730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17731" type="x-p"/> But if they obey not - This also is a general rule, from which, in the course of Providence, there are only few, and those only apparent, deviations. Instead of they shall perish by the sword, the meaning of the Hebrew בשלח יעברו beshelach yaaboru, is, "By a dart they shall pass by." They shall be in continual dangers, and often fall before they have lived out half their days. Mr. Good translates: They pass by as an arrow. The Vulgate: Transibunt per gladium.
