"They shall pass away by the sword."
entries.0cf2a2b5fafa9203739f5dd6bc55d0736420f127: <hi type="bold">Verse 13</hi> <div eID="gen17731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17732" type="x-p"/> But the hypocrites in heart - חנפי chanphey, the profligates, the impious, those who have neither the form nor the power of godliness. The hypocrite is he who has the form but not the power, though he wishes to be thought as inwardly righteous as he is outwardly correct; and he takes up the profession of religion only to serve secular ends. This is not the meaning of the word in the book of Job, where it frequently occurs. <div eID="gen17732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17733" type="x-p"/> They cry not - "Though he binds them, yet they cry not." They are too obstinate to humble themselves even under the mighty hand of God.
entries.4773b4ca97b598dbecab125134ef71943c99203b: <hi type="bold">Verse 14</hi> <div eID="gen17733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17734" type="x-p"/> They die in youth - Exactly what the psalmist says, "Bloody and deceitful men shall not live out half their days," <reference osisRef="Psa.55.23">Psa 55:23</reference>. Literally, the words of Elihu are, "They shall die in the youth of their soul." <div eID="gen17734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17735" type="x-p"/> Their life is among the unclean - בקדשים bakedeshim, among the whores, harlots, prostitutes, and sodomites. In this sense the word is used, though it also signifies consecrated persons; but we know that in idolatry characters of this kind were consecrated to Baal and Ashtaroth, Venus, Priapus, etc. Mr. Good translates the rabble. The Septuagint: Their life shalt be wounded by the angels.
entries.7b4b4b8eb831d8a1dacd433e34b79fdc95ad6ef5: <hi type="bold">Verse 15</hi> <div eID="gen17735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17736" type="x-p"/> And openeth their ears in oppression - He will let them know for what end they are afflicted, and why he permits them to be oppressed. The word יגל yigel might be translated he shall make them exult, or sing with joy, in oppression; like the three Hebrews in the burning fiery furnace.
entries.212bae9c3c6a95923ac6e5bc8fbf585f37f019ba: <hi type="bold">Verse 16</hi> <div eID="gen17736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17737" type="x-p"/> Even so would he have removed thee - If thou hadst turned to, obeyed, and served him, thy present state would have been widely different from what it is.
entries.a768d1ad6cd364b539ec9d02e99f800ba2b75068: <hi type="bold">Verse 17</hi> <div eID="gen17737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17738" type="x-p"/> But thou hast fulfilled the judgment of the wicked - As thou art acting like the wicked, so God deals with thee as he deals with them. Elihu is not a whit behind Job's other friends. None of them seems to have known any thing of the permission given by God to Satan to afflict and torment an innocent man.
entries.f3550cc7ebd74f99195bf256d479538a330f65c7: <hi type="bold">Verse 18</hi> <div eID="gen17738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17739" type="x-p"/> Because there is wrath - This is a time in which God is punishing the wicked; take heed lest thou be cut off in a moment. Redeem the time; the days are evil. <div eID="gen17739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17740" type="x-p"/> Then a great ransom - When he determines to destroy, who can save?
entries.af98f327ff6f1ac9776e52917805bad15dd5f290: <hi type="bold">Verse 20</hi> <div eID="gen17740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17741" type="x-p"/> Desire not the night - Thou hast wished for death; (here called night); desire it not; leave that with God. If he hear thee, and send death, thou mayest be cut off in a way at which thy soul would shudder.
entries.3ce40e2d0386d0fb37aad0113a7622ef86a46186: <hi type="bold">Verse 21</hi> <div eID="gen17741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17742" type="x-p"/> Regard not iniquity - It is sinful to entertain such wishes; it is an insult to the providence of God. He sends affliction; he knows this to be best for thee: but thou hast preferred death to affliction, thereby setting thy wisdom against the wisdom of God. Many in affliction, long for death; and yet they are not prepared to appear before God! What madness is this! If he takes them at their wish, they are ruined for ever. Affliction may be the means of their salvation; the wished-for death, of their eternal destruction.
entries.8ecdc22d4bfaf9f493a469247c17e2bc192718c9: <hi type="bold">Verse 22</hi> <div eID="gen17742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17743" type="x-p"/> God exalteth by his power - He has brought thee low, but he can raise thee up. Thou art not yet out of the reach of his mercy. Thy affliction is a proof that he acts towards thee as a merciful Parent. He knows what is best to be done; he teaches thee how thou shouldst suffer and improve. Why sin against his kindness? Who can teach like him?
entries.14652b0e08891f7b079dc0f12f79f0723893b33b: <hi type="bold">Verse 23</hi> <div eID="gen17743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17744" type="x-p"/> Who hath enjoined him his way - Has God taken instructions from any man how he shall govern the world? <div eID="gen17744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17745" type="x-p"/> Thou hast wrought iniquity? - Who can prove, in the whole compass of the creation, that there is one thing imperfect, superabundant, or out of its place? Who can show that there is, in the course of the Divine providence, one unrighteous, cruel, or unwise act? All the cunning and wickedness of man have never been able to find out the smallest flaw in the work of God.
entries.cfb7f0bb047ecf0e8a97a53dcde82195829afab7: <hi type="bold">Verse 24</hi> <div eID="gen17745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17746" type="x-p"/> Remember that thou magnify his work - Take this into consideration; instead of fretting against the dispensations of Divine providence, and quarrelling with thy Maker, attentively survey his works; consider the operation of his hands; and see the proofs of his wisdom in the plan of all, of his power in the production and support of all, and of his goodness in the end for which all have been made, and to which every operation in nature most obviously tends; and then magnify his work. Speak of him as thou shalt find; let the visible works of thy Maker prove to thee his eternal power and Godhead, and let nature lead thee to the Creator.
entries.b3a5e75ebaf283183976289cfa0c4853bb34100a: <hi type="bold">Verse 25</hi> <div eID="gen17746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17747" type="x-p"/> Every man may see it - He who says he can examine the earth with a philosophic eye, and the heavens with the eye of an astronomer, and yet says he cannot see in them a system of infinite skill and contrivance, must be ignorant of science, or lie against his conscience, and be utterly unworthy of confidence or respect.
entries.03f760108a4a1d3871440004796cc49bcc699fed: <hi type="bold">Verse 26</hi> <div eID="gen17747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17748" type="x-p"/> God is great - He is omnipotent. <div eID="gen17748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17749" type="x-p"/> We know him not - He is unsearchable. <div eID="gen17749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17750" type="x-p"/> Neither can the number of his years be searched out - He is eternal. <div eID="gen17750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17751" type="x-p"/> These three propositions are an ample foundation for endless disquisition. As to paraphrase and comment, they need none in this place; they are too profound, comprehensive, and sublime.
entries.df94c155cff22c652d5f8dd1a29e923c8817c25a: <hi type="bold">Verse 27</hi> <div eID="gen17751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17752" type="x-p"/> He maketh small the drops of water - This appears simply to refer to evaporation, and perhaps it would be better to translate יגרע yegara, "he exhales;" detaches the smallest particles of the aqueous mass from the surface in order to form clouds, as reservoirs for the purpose of furnishing rain for the watering of the earth. God is seen in little things, as well as great things; and the inconceivably little, as well as the stupendously great, are equally the work of Omnipotence. <div eID="gen17752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17753" type="x-p"/> They pour down rain - These exceedingly minute drops or vapor become collected in clouds; and then, when agitated by winds, etc. many particles being united, they become too heavy to be sustained by the air in which they before were suspended, and so fall down in rain, which is either a mist, a drizzle, a shower, a storm, or a waterspout, according to the influence of different winds, or the presence and quantum of the electric fluid. And all this is proportioned, לאדו le-edo, "to its vapor," to the quantity of the fluid evaporated and condensed into clouds.
entries.c40202af1f4460782c0114e7bcfeccf4454cdc8a: <hi type="bold">Verse 28</hi> <div eID="gen17753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17754" type="x-p"/> Which the clouds do drop - In proportion to the evaporation will be the clouds or masses of volatilized and suspended vapor; and in proportion to this will be the quantum of rain which in different forms will fall upon the earth. There is a remarkable addition to this verse in the Septuagint. I shall insert the whole verse: Ῥυησονται παλαιωματα, εσκιασε δε νεφη επι αμυθητῳ βροτῳ· ὡραν εθετο κτηνεσιν, οιδασι δε κοιτης ταξιν· επι τουτοις πασιν ουκ εξισταται σου ἡ διανοια, ουδε διαλλασσεται σου ἡ καρδια απο σωματος; "The rains descend, and the clouds cover with their shadows multitudes of men: he hath appointed to animals to know the order of their dwellings. At the contemplation of these things is not thy mind transported, and thy heart ready to part from thy body?"
entries.6b943c4c5dae3a4a4648fd2e5248351be1645216: <hi type="bold">Verse 29</hi> <div eID="gen17754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17755" type="x-p"/> Can any understand the spreadings of the clouds - Though the vapor appear to be fortuitously raised, and subject, when suspended in the atmosphere, to innumerable accidents, to different winds and currents which might drive it all to the sandy deserts, or direct its course so that it should fall again into the great deep from which it has been exhaled, without watering and refreshing the earth; yet so does the good and wise providence of God manage this matter, that every part of the arable terrene surface receives an ample supply; and in every place, where requisite, it may be truly said that "The rain cometh down, and the snow from heaven, and water the earth, and cause it to bring forth and bud, that it may minister seed to the sower, and bread to the eater." In Egypt, where there is little or no rain, the earth is watered by the annual inundation of the Nile; there, because this system of evaporation is not necessary, it does not exist. Who can account for this economy? How are these clouds so judiciously and effectually spread through the atmosphere, so as to supply the wants of the earth, of men, and of cattle? I ask, with Elihu, "Who can understand the spreadings of these clouds?" And I should like to see that volunteer in the solution of paradoxes who would step forward and say, I am the man. <div eID="gen17755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17756" type="x-p"/> The noise of his tabernacle? - By the tabernacle we may understand the whole firmament or atmospheric expansion; the place where the Almighty seems more particularly to dwell; whence he sends forth the rain of his strength, and the thunder of his power. The noise must refer to the blowing of winds and tempests. or to the claps, peals, and rattling of thunder, by means of the electric fluid.
entries.e78d74916473f79a3dbccf588b93061fe35540a3: <hi type="bold">Verse 30</hi> <div eID="gen17756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17757" type="x-p"/> He spreadeth his light upon it - Or, as Mr. Good translates, "He throweth forth from it his flash." These two verses may both have an allusion to the sudden rarefaction of that part of the atmosphere whence the thunder proceeds, by the agency of the electric fluid; the rushing in of the air on each side to restore the equilibrium, which the passage of the fire had before destroyed. The noise produced by this sudden rushing in of the air, as well as that occasioned by the ignition of the hydrogen gas, which is one of the constituents of water, is the thunder of his tabernacle, viz., the atmosphere, where God appears, in such cases, to be manifesting his presence and his power. Elihu says that God spreadeth his light upon it. This is spoken in reference to the flashes and coruscations of lightning in the time of thunder storms, when, even in a dark night, a sudden flash illuminates for a moment the surface of the earth under that place. <div eID="gen17757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17758" type="x-p"/> And covereth the bottom of the sea - He doth whatsoever it pleaseth him in the heavens above, in the earth beneath, in the sea, and in all deep places. Yea, the depths of the sea are as much under his control and influence as the atmosphere, and its whole collection of vapours, meteors, and galvanic and electric fluids.
entries.775260c738c9fc76485348243e9c265d1b8821c1: <hi type="bold">Verse 31</hi> <div eID="gen17758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17759" type="x-p"/> By them judgeth he the people - He makes storms, tempests, winds, hurricanes, tornadoes, thunder and lightning, drought and inundation, the instruments of his justice, to punish rebellious nations. <div eID="gen17759" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17760" type="x-p"/> He giveth meat in abundance - Though by these he punishes offenders, yet through the same, as instruments, he provides for the wants of men and animals in general. Storms, tempests, and hurricanes, agitate the lower regions of the atmosphere, disperse noxious vapours, and thus render it fit for respiration; and without these it would soon become a stagnant, putrid, and deadly mass, in which neither animals could live, nor vegetables thrive. And by dews, rains, snows, frosts, winds, cold, and heat, he fructifies the earth, and causes it to bring forth abundantly, so that every thing living is filled with plenteousness. Some critics translate this latter clause thus: - He passeth sentence amain. I cannot see this meaning in the original words. Not one of the versions has so understood them; nor does this translation, supposing even that the Hebrew would bear it, give so fine and so elegant an idea as that of the common version. I always feel reluctant to give a sense in any case that is not supported in some of its parts by any of the ancient versions, and more especially when it is contrary to the whole of them; and still more particularly when opposed to the Arabic, which in the Book of Job, containing so many Arabisms, I consider to be of very great importance.
entries.b72849737266efaa5b5a5b9eb78c9134cb221e7d: <hi type="bold">Verse 32</hi> <div eID="gen17760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17761" type="x-p"/> With clouds he covereth the light - This is all extraordinary saying, על כפים כמה אור al cappayim kissah or, which Mr. Good translates, "He brandisheth the blaze athwart the concave." The Vulgate, with which all the other versions less or more agree, has, In manibus abscondit lucem, "In his hands he hideth the light;" or, more literally, "By the hollow of his hands (כפים cappayim) he concealeth the light, (אור or,") the fountain of light, i.e., the Sun. <div eID="gen17761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17762" type="x-p"/> And commandeth it not to shine by the cloud that cometh betwixt - I am afraid this is no translation of the original. Old Coverdale is better: - And at his commandement it commeth agayne; which is a near copy of the Vulgate. Here again Mr. Good departs from all the versions, both ancient and modern, by translating thus: - "And launcheth his penetrating bolt." Dr. Stock, in my opinion, comes nearer the original and the versions in his translation: - "And giveth charge as to what it shall meet." <div eID="gen17762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17763" type="x-p"/> The mending of the text by conjecture, to which we should only recur in desperate necessity, has furnished Mr. Good and Reiske with the above translation. For my own part, I must acknowledge an extreme difficulty both here and in the concluding verse, on which I am unwilling to lay a correcting hand. I think something of the doctrine of eclipses is here referred to; the defect of the solar light, by the interposition of the moon. So in the time of an eclipse God is represented as covering the body of the sun with the hollow of his hand, and thus obscuring the solar light, and then removing his hand so as to permit it to re-illuminate the earth. <div eID="gen17763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17764" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good gets his translation by dividing the words in a different manner from the present text. I shall give both: - <div eID="gen17764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17765" type="x-p"/> Hebrew: ויצו עליה במפגיע <div eID="gen17765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17766" type="x-p"/> Vayetsav aleyha bemaphgia <div eID="gen17766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17767" type="x-p"/> Mr. Good: ויצוע ליהב מפגיע <div eID="gen17767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17768" type="x-p"/> Veyezvo liahbe mapegio. <div eID="gen17768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17769" type="x-p"/> Of which he learnedly contends, "And launcheth his penetrating bolt," is the literal sense. The change here made, to produce the above meaning, is not a violent one; and I must leave the reader to judge of its importance.
entries.263cf4a3c78c7e2bf40303a8af2830a82fc8bbd3: <hi type="bold">Verse 33</hi> <div eID="gen17769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17770" type="x-p"/> The noise thereof showeth concerning it, the cattle also concerning the vapor - I think this translation very unhappy. I shall give each hemistich in the original: - יגיד עליו רעו <div eID="gen17770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17771" type="x-p"/> Yaggid alaiv reo מקנה אף על עולה <div eID="gen17771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17772" type="x-p"/> Mikneh aph al oleh. <div eID="gen17772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17773" type="x-p"/> I think this may be translated without any violence to any word in the text: - <div eID="gen17773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17774" type="x-p"/> Its loud noise (or his thunder) shall proclaim concerning him; <div eID="gen17774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17775" type="x-p"/> A magazine of wrath against iniquity. <div eID="gen17775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen17776" type="x-p"/> This is literal, and gives, in my opinion, a proper meaning of the passage, and one in strict connection with the context. And it is worthy of remark that every wicked man trembles at the noise of thunder and the flash of lightning, and considers this a treasury of Divine wrath, emphatically called among us the artillery of the skies; and whenever the noise is heard, it is considered the voice of God. Thus the thunder declares concerning him. The next chapter, which is a continuation of the subject here, confirms and illustrates this meaning. For יגיד yaggid, Houbigant reads יניד yanid; and for מקנה mikneh, מקנאת mikkinath; and translates thus: "He agitates with himself his thunder, from the indignation of his wrath against iniquity."  <chapter eID="Job.36"/> <div eID="gen17776" type="x-p"/>

entries.caf8d9fc96ee81fa2ffe65e797b24dfd1b8a498a: <reference osisRef="Job.36.1-Job.4.1">Job 36:1-4   1</reference>  Then Elihu continued and said:   2  Suffer me a little, and I will inform thee, <div eID="gen8492" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8493" type="x-p"/> For there is something still to be said for Eloah.   3  I will fetch my knowledge from afar, <div eID="gen8493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8494" type="x-p"/> And to my Creator will I ascribe right.   4  For truly my words are not lies, <div eID="gen8494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8495" type="x-p"/> One perfect in knowledge stands before thee. <div eID="gen8495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8496" type="x-p"/> Elihu’s preceding three speeches were introduced by ויּען; this fourth, in honour of the number three, is introduced only as a continuation of the others. Job is to wait yet a little while, for he still has (= עוד לּי), or: there still are, words in favour of Eloah; i.e., what may be said in vindication of God against Job’s complaints and accusations is not yet exhausted. This appears to be the only instance of the Aramaic כּתּר being taken up as Hebr.; whereas הוּה, <hi type="italic">nunciare</hi> (Arab. <hi type="italic">wḥâ</hi>, I, IV), is a poetic Aramaism occurring even in <reference osisRef="Ps.19.3">Psa 19:3</reference> (comp. on the construction <reference osisRef="Job.32.6">Job 32:6</reference>); and זעיר (a diminutive form, after the manner of the Arab. <hi type="italic">zu‛air</hi>) belongs in <reference osisRef="Isa.28.10">Isa 28:10</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.28.13">Isa 28:13</reference> to the popular language (of Jerusalem), but is here used poetically. The verb נשׂא, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.3">Job 36:3</reference></hi>, is not to be understood according to נשׂא משׁל, but according to 1Ki 10:11; and למרחוק signifies, as also <reference osisRef="Job.39.29">Job 39:29</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.37.26">Isa 37:26</reference>, <hi type="italic">e longinquo,</hi> viz., out of the wide realm of history and nature. The expression נתן צדק follows the analogy of (עז) נתן כבוד. דּעה, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.4">Job 36:4</reference></hi>, interchanges with the דּע which belongs exclusively to Elihu, since Elihu styles himself תּמים דּעות, as <reference osisRef="Job.37.16">Job 37:16</reference> God תּמים דּעים (comp. <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.3">1Sa 2:3</reference>, אל דּעות). תמים in this combination with דעות cannot be intended of purity of character; but as Elihu there attributes absolute perfection of knowledge in every direction to God, so here, in reference to the theodicy which he opposes to Job, he claims faultlessness and clearness of perception.
entries.0e4ee22b765237cd2782a16b7410fd4df9ad6d9f: <reference osisRef="Job.36.5-Job.7.5">Job 36:5-7   5</reference>  Behold, God is mighty, and yet doth not act scornfully, <div eID="gen8496" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8497" type="x-p"/> Mighty in power of understanding.   6  He preserveth not the life of the ungodly, <div eID="gen8497" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8498" type="x-p"/> And to the afflicted He giveth right.   7  He withdraweth not His eyes from the righteous, <div eID="gen8498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8499" type="x-p"/> But with kings on the throne <div eID="gen8499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8500" type="x-p"/> He establisheth them for ever, and they are exalted. <div eID="gen8500" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8501" type="x-p"/> The obj. that must be mentally supplied to ימאס ולא is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.42.6">Job 42:6</reference>, to be derived from the connection. The idea of the verb is, as in <reference osisRef="Job.8.20">Job 8:20</reference> : He is exalted, without however looking down disdainfully (<hi type="italic">non despicit</hi>) from His height, or more definitely: without setting Himself above the justice due to even the meanest of His creatures - great in power of heart (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.34.33">Job 34:33</reference> אנשׁי לבב, Arab. <hi type="italic">ûlû - l - elbâb</hi>), i.e., understanding (νοῦς πνεῦμα), to see through right and wrong everywhere and altogether. <reference osisRef="Job.36.6">Job 36:6</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.7">Job 36:7</reference> describe how His rule among men evinces this not merely outward but spiritual superiority coupled with condescension to the lowly. The notion of the object, ואת־מלכים לכּסּא (as <reference osisRef="Isa.9.11">Isa 9:11</reference> the subject), becomes the more distinctly prominent by virtue of the <hi type="italic">fut. consec.</hi> which follows like a conclusion, and takes it up again. Ewald thinks this explanation contrary to the accents and the structure of the sentence itself; but it is perfectly consistent with the former, and indisputably syntactic (Ges. §129, 2, <hi type="italic">b</hi>, and Ew. himself, §344, <hi type="italic">b</hi>). <reference osisRef="Ps.9.5">Psa 9:5</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.132.12">Psa 132:12</reference>, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.1">Isa 47:1</reference>, shows how לכסא is intended (He causes them to sit upon the throne). <reference osisRef="Job.5.11">Job 5:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.2.8">1Sa 2:8</reference>; Psa 113:7. are parallel passages.
entries.ccbb618c52f59f71eec9112b160fd05f9b0560d0: <reference osisRef="Job.36.8-Job.10.8">Job 36:8-10   8</reference>  And if they are bound with chains, <div eID="gen8501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8502" type="x-p"/> Holden in cords of affliction:   9  Then He declareth to them their doing <div eID="gen8502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8503" type="x-p"/> And their transgressions, that they have been vainglorious; 10  Then He openeth their ear to warning, <div eID="gen8503" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8504" type="x-p"/> And commandeth them to turn from iniquity. <div eID="gen8504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8505" type="x-p"/> The subj. is in no case the רשׁעים (Hahn), but the צדיקים, or those who are as susceptible to discipline as it is needful to them, just as in Ps 107, which in general presents many instances for an extensive comparison with the speeches of Elihu. The chains, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference></hi>, are meant literally, and the bands, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.8">Job 36:8</reference></hi>, figuratively; the Psalmist couples both in אסירי עני וברזל, Psa 107:10. The conclusion begins with <reference osisRef="Job.36.9">Job 36:9</reference>, and is repeated in another application, Job 36:10. פּעל in the sense of <hi type="italic">maleficium</hi>, as Arab. <hi type="italic">fa‛alat</hi>, recalls מעשׂה, <hi type="italic">facinus</hi>, Job 33:17. כּי, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.9">Job 36:9</reference></hi>, as in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.10">Job 36:10</reference></hi>, an objective <hi type="italic">quod</hi>. It is not translated, however, <hi type="italic">quod invaluerint</hi> (Rosenm.), which is opposed to the most natural sense of the <hi type="italic">Hithpa.,</hi> but according to <reference osisRef="Job.15.25">Job 15:25</reference> : <hi type="italic">quod sese extulerint.</hi> מוּסר, παιδεία, <hi type="italic">disciplina</hi>, interchanges here with the more rare מסר used in <reference osisRef="Job.33.16">Job 33:16</reference>; there we have already also met with the phrase גּלה אזן, to uncover the ear, i.e., to open. אמר כּי corresponds to the Arab. <hi type="italic">amara an</hi> (<hi type="italic">bi - an</hi>), to command that. The fundamental thought of Elihu here once again comes unmistakeably to view: the sufferings of the righteous are well-meant chastisements, which are to wean them from the sins into which through carnal security they have fallen - a warning from God to penitence, designed to work their good.
entries.de6ccdb4871b7fdbed0a315a8cd0aeac299a9c6e: <reference osisRef="Job.36.11-Job.12.11">Job 36:11-12 11</reference>  If they hear and yield, <div eID="gen8505" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8506" type="x-p"/> They pass their days in prosperity <div eID="gen8506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8507" type="x-p"/> And their years in pleasure. 12  And if they hear not, <div eID="gen8507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8508" type="x-p"/> They pass away by the bow <div eID="gen8508" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8509" type="x-p"/> And expire in lack of knowledge. <div eID="gen8509" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8510" type="x-p"/> Since a declaration of the divine will has preceded in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.10">Job 36:10</reference></hi>, it is more natural to take ויעבדוּ in the sense of <hi type="italic">obsequi</hi>, to do the will of another (as 1Ki 12:7, comp. מעבּד from עבד in the generalized sense of <hi type="italic">facere</hi>), than, with Umbr., in the sense of <hi type="italic">colere scil. Deum</hi> (as <reference osisRef="Isa.19.23">Isa 19:23</reference>, Arab. <hi type="italic">‛âbid</hi>, one who reveres God, a godly person). Instead of יבלּוּ, <reference osisRef="Isa.65.22">Isa 65:22</reference> (on which the Masora observes לית, i.e., “nowhere else”) and <reference osisRef="Job.21.13">Job 21:13</reference> <hi type="italic">Chethîb</hi>, 'it is here without dispute יכלּוּ (Targ. ישׁלּמוּן, <hi type="italic">peragent</hi>, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.43.27">Eze 43:27</reference>). נעימים is, as <reference osisRef="Ps.16.6">Psa 16:6</reference>, a neutral masc.: <hi type="italic">amoena</hi>. On עבר בשׁלח, to precipitate one’s self into the weapon, i.e., to incur peremptory punishment, comp. Job 33:18. On בבלי דעת comp. <reference osisRef="Job.35.16">Job 35:16</reference>; Job 4:21. Impenitence changes affliction, which is intended to be a means of rescue, into total destruction; yet there are some who will not be warned and affrighted by it.
entries.0ce60ee7e41a4ca88980a959ab017b7981c6a133: <reference osisRef="Job.36.13-Job.15.13">Job 36:13-15 13</reference>  Yet the hypocrites in heart cherish wrath, <div eID="gen8510" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8511" type="x-p"/> They cry not when He hath chained them. 14  Thus their soul dieth in the vigour of youth, <div eID="gen8511" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8512" type="x-p"/> And their life is like that of the unclean. 15  Yet He delivereth the sufferer by his affliction, <div eID="gen8512" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8513" type="x-p"/> And openeth their ear by oppression. <div eID="gen8513" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8514" type="x-p"/> He who is angry with God in his affliction, and does not humbly pray to Him, shows thereby that he is a חנף, one estranged from God (on the idea of the root, vid., i. 216), and not a צדיק. This connection renders it natural to understand not the divine wrath by אף: θησαυρίζουσιν ὀργήν (Rosenm. after <reference osisRef="Rom.2.5">Rom 2:5</reference>), or: they heap up wrath upon themselves (Wolfson, who supplies עליהם), but the impatience, discontent, and murmuring of man himself: they cherish or harbour wrath, viz., בּלבּם (comp. <reference osisRef="Job.22.22">Job 22:22</reference>, where שׁים בלב signifies to take to heart, but at the same time to preserve in the heart). Used thus absolutely, שׂים signifies elsewhere in the book, to give attention to, <reference osisRef="Job.4.20">Job 4:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.24.12">Job 24:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.34.23">Job 34:23</reference>, or (as Arab. <hi type="italic">wḍ‛</hi>) to lay down a pledge; here it signifies <hi type="italic">reponunt s. recondunt</hi> (with an implied <hi type="italic">in ipsis</hi>), as also Arab. <hi type="italic">šâm , fut. i,</hi> to conceal with the idea of sinking into (<hi type="italic">immittentem</hi>), e.g., the sword in the sheath. With תּמת, for ותּמת (<reference osisRef="Isa.50.2">Isa 50:2</reference>) or ותמת, the punishment which issues forth undistinguished from this frustration of the divine purpose of grace follows ἀσυνδέτως, as e.g., Hos 7:16. חיּה interchanges with נפשׁ, as <reference osisRef="Job.33.22">Job 33:22</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.33.28">Job 33:28</reference>; נער (likewise a favourite word with Elihu) is intended just as <reference osisRef="Job.33.25">Job 33:25</reference>, and in the <reference osisRef="Ps.88.16">Psa 88:16</reference>, which resembles both the Elihu section and the rest of the book. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> of בּקּדשׁים has the sense of <hi type="italic">aeque ac</hi> (Targ. היך), as <reference osisRef="Job.34.36">Job 34:36</reference>, comp. תּחת, Job 34:26. Jer. translates <hi type="italic">inter effeminatos;</hi> for קדשׁים (heathenish, equivalent to קדושׁים, as כּמרים, heathenish, equivalent to כּהנים) are the consecrated men, who yielded themselves up, like the women in honour of the deity, to passive, prematurely-enervating incontinence (vid., Keil on <reference osisRef="Deut.23.18">Deu 23:18</reference>), a heathenish abomination prevailing now and again even in Israel (1Ki 14:24; 1Ki 15:12; 1Ki 22:47), which was connected with the worship of Astarte and Baal that was transferred from Syria, and to which allusion is here made, in accordance with the scene of the book. For the sufferer, on the other hand, who suffers not merely of necessity, but willingly, this his suffering is a means of rescue and moral purification. Observe the play upon the words יחלּץ and בּלחץ. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> in both instances is, in accordance with Elihu’s fundamental thought, the <hi type="italic">Beth instrum</hi>.
entries.9b039b47c126b3bdda4d353f45b74687151b1f47: <reference osisRef="Job.36.16-Job.18.16">Job 36:16-18 16</reference>  And He even bringeth thee out of the jaws of distress <div eID="gen8514" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8515" type="x-p"/> To a broad place, whose ground hath no straitness, <div eID="gen8515" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8516" type="x-p"/> And the adorning of thy table shall be full of fatness. 17  Yet thou art become full of the judging of the evil-doer: <div eID="gen8516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8517" type="x-p"/> Judging and judgment lay hold on one another! 18  For let not anger indeed entice thee to scorning, <div eID="gen8517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8518" type="x-p"/> And let not the greatness of the ransom mislead thee. <div eID="gen8518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8519" type="x-p"/> With <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference></hi> Elihu passes over to the application to Job of what he said in the preceding strophe. Since it is usual to place אף (like גּם and אך) at the beginning of the sentence, although not belonging to the member of the sentence which immediately follows, ואף הסיתך for והסית אף אתך cannot be remarkable. The <hi type="italic">praet</hi>. הסיתך is not promissory, but Elihu says with what design God has decreed the present suffering for Job. הסית מן is like <reference osisRef="2Chr.18.31">2Ch 18:31</reference> : out of distress (צר for צר by <hi type="italic">Rebia magnum</hi>), which has him in its jaws, and threatens to swallow him, God brings him away to great prosperity; a thought which Elihu expresses in the imagery of the Psalms of a broad place and a bountiful table (comp. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.4.2">Psa 4:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.23.5">Psa 23:5</reference>). רחב is locative, and לא־מוּצק תּחתּיה is either a relative clause: whose beneath (ground) is not straitened, no-straitness (in which case מוּצק would not be <hi type="italic">constr</hi>. from the <hi type="italic">n. hophal.</hi> מוּצק, Isa.Isa 9:1, but <hi type="italic">absol</hi>. after the form מחנק, <reference osisRef="Job.7.15">Job 7:15</reference>, Ew. §160, <hi type="italic">c</hi>, Anm. 4), Saad. Arab. <hi type="italic">lâ ḍı̂q fı̂ mûḍ‛hâ</hi> (<hi type="italic">cujus in loco non angustiae</hi>); or it is virtually an adj.: without (לא = בּלא, as <reference osisRef="Job.34.24">Job 34:24</reference>), comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.12.24">Job 12:24</reference>) straitness of what is beneath them, <hi type="italic">eorum quae sub se habet</hi> (comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.28.5">Job 28:5</reference>). רחב is <hi type="italic">fem.,</hi> like רחוב, Dan 9:25. A special clause takes the place of the locative, <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference> : and the settling or spreading, i.e., the provision (from נוּח, to come down gradually, to seat one’s self) of thy table shall be full of fatness. מלא (whether it be adj. or verb) is treated by attraction, according to the gender of the governed noun; and it is unnecessary, with Rosenm. and others, to derive נחת from נחת (Aram. for ירד). <div eID="gen8519" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8520" type="x-p"/> In <reference osisRef="Job.36.17">Job 36:17</reference>, דּין is intended of Job’s negative judgment concerning God and His dealings (comp. <reference osisRef="Ps.76.9">Psa 76:9</reference>, where it signifies a judicial decision, and <reference osisRef="Prov.22.10">Pro 22:10</reference>, where it signifies a wrangling refusal of a fair decision). <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.17">Job 36:17</reference></hi> is not a conditional clause (Hahn), in which case the <hi type="italic">praet. hypothet</hi>. would have a prominent position, but an adversative predicative clause: but (nevertheless) thou art full of the judging of the evil-doer (evil judging); after which, just as ἀσυνδέτως as <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.14">Job 36:14</reference></hi>, the sad issue in which this judging after the manner of evil-doers results is expressed: such judging and judgment border closely upon one another. Röd., Dietr., and Schlottm. have wrongly reproduced this idea, discerned by Ges., when they translate: judgment and sentence (guilt and punishment) shall seize thee. יתמכוּ, <hi type="italic">prehendunt scil. se</hi> (Ebr.: put forth the hand), is used like the Aram. סמך, to draw nearer, fasten together (Rabb. סמוּך, near at hand), Arab. <hi type="italic">tamâsaka</hi> (from Arab. <hi type="italic">msk</hi> = סמך, as e.g., <hi type="italic">hanash</hi> = נחשׁ). In <reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference> we leave the signification thick milk or cream (חמה = חמאה, as <reference osisRef="Job.29.6">Job 29:6</reference>) to those who persuade themselves that cream can be metaphorically equivalent to superfluity (Ew., Hirz., Vaih., Hlgst.). Renan’s translation: <hi type="italic">N'espère pas détourner la colère de Dieu par une amende,</hi> we also leave as a simple puzzle to its discoverer, who, with this one exception, is destitute of thoughts proper to the book of Job. In general, the thought, “do not imagine by riches, by a great ransom, to be able to satisfy the claims of God,” is altogether out of place here. Moreover, חמה, which, as e.g., דּאגה, <reference osisRef="Prov.12.25">Pro 12:25</reference> (Ew. §174, <hi type="italic">g</hi>), is construed as <hi type="italic">masc.,</hi> cannot be understood of God’s wrath, since the poet by הסית will not at one time have ascribed to God a well-meant incitation, at another an enticement <hi type="italic">in malam partem.</hi> That which allures is Job’s own חמה, and that not the excitement of his affliction (Hahn), but of his passion; comp. אף, Job 36:13. שׂפק is, however, to be explained according to <reference osisRef="Job.34.37">Job 34:37</reference>, comp. <reference osisRef="Job.27.23">Job 27:23</reference> (clapping of hands = derision); and כּפר signifies reconciliation or expiation, as Job 33:24. Elihu admonishes Job not to allow himself to be drawn by the heat of passion into derision, or to deride; nor to be allured from the right way by the ransom which is required of him as the price of restoration to happiness, viz., humble submission to the divine chastisement, as though this ransom were exceeding great. The connection is clear: an adverse verdict (דּין) and condemnation (משׁפּט) are closely connected; for (כּי) hastiness of temper, let it not (פּן( ton ti ) lead thee astray ... thou wouldst not escape the judgment of God!
entries.7b9ed1cfa6bb33e0a21a8732a6455032a762688f: <reference osisRef="Job.36.19-Job.21.19">Job 36:19-21 19</reference>  Shall thy crying place thee beyond distress, <div eID="gen8520" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8521" type="x-p"/> And all the efforts of strength? 20  Long not for the night to come, <div eID="gen8521" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8522" type="x-p"/> Which shall remove people from their place! 21  Take heed, incline not to evil; <div eID="gen8522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> For this thou hast desired more than affliction. <div eID="gen8523" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8524" type="x-p"/> Those expositors who found in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.18">Job 36:18</reference></hi> the warning, that Job should not imagine that he would be able to redeem himself from judgment by a large ransom, go on to explain: will He esteem thy riches? (Farisol, Rosenm., Umbr., Carey, Ebr., and others); or: will thy riches suffice? (Hirz., Schlottm.); or some other way (Ew.). But apart from the want of connection of this insinuation, which is otherwise not mentioned in the book, and apart from the violence which must be done to היערך to accommodate it to it, שׁוּע, although it might, as the abstract of שׁוע, <reference osisRef="Job.34.19">Job 34:19</reference>, signify wealth (comp. Arab. <hi type="italic">sa‛at , amplitudo</hi>), is, however, according to the usage of the language (vid., <reference osisRef="Job.30.24">Job 30:24</reference>), so far as we can trace it, a secondary form of שׁוע (שׁועה), a cry for help; and Job 35:9., <reference osisRef="Job.36.13">Job 36:13</reference>, and other passages, also point to this signification. What follows is still less appropriate to this thought of ransom; Hirz. translates: Oh, not God and all the treasures of wealth! But בּצר is nowhere equivalent to בּצר, <reference osisRef="Job.22.24">Job 22:24</reference>; but צר, <reference osisRef="Job.36.16">Job 36:16</reference>, signifies distress; and the expression לא בצר, in a condition devoid of distress, is like לא בחכמה, <reference osisRef="Job.4.21">Job 4:21</reference>, and לא ביד, Job 34:20. Finally, אמּיץ כּח signifies mighty in physical strength, <reference osisRef="Job.9.4">Job 9:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.9.19">Job 9:19</reference>, and מאמצּי־כח strong proofs of strength, not “treasures of wealth.” Stick. correctly interprets: “Will thy wild raging cry, then, and all thine exertions, as a warrior puts them forth in the tumult of battle to work his way out, put thee where there is an open space?” but the figure of a warrior is, with Hahn, to be rejected; ערך is only a nice word for שׁית שׂים, to place, set up, Job 37:19.
entries.0de322bf5516a87bbc958becb4c49123a9e0d958: Job 36:22-25 22  Behold, God acteth loftily in His strength; <div eID="gen8525" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8526" type="x-p"/> Who is a teacher like unto Him? 23  Who hath appointed Him His way, <div eID="gen8526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8527" type="x-p"/> And who dare say: Thou doest iniquity!? 24  Remember that thou magnify His doing, <div eID="gen8527" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8528" type="x-p"/> Which men have sung. 25  All men delight in it, <div eID="gen8528" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8529" type="x-p"/> Mortal man looketh upon it from afar. <div eID="gen8529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8530" type="x-p"/> Most modern expositors, after the lxx δυνάστης, give אמת the signification lord, by comparing the Arab. <hi type="italic">mar - un</hi> (<hi type="italic">imru - un</hi>), Syr. <hi type="italic">mor</hi> (with the art. <hi type="italic">moro</hi>) or <hi type="italic">more</hi> (with the art. <hi type="italic">morjo</hi>), Chald. מרא, Talmud. מר (comp. Philo, ii. 522, <hi type="italic">ed. Mangey:</hi> οὃτως, viz., μάριν φασὶ τὸν κύριον ὀνομάζεστηαι παρὰ Σύροις), with it; but Rosenm., Arnh., Löwenthal, Wolfson, and Schlottm., after the Targ., Syr., and Jer., rightly abide by the signification: teacher. For (1) אמת (from הורה, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.8">Psa 25:8</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.25.12">Psa 25:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.32.8">Psa 32:8</reference>) has no etymological connection with mr (of מרא, Arab. <hi type="italic">maru'a , opimum, robustum esse</hi>); (2) it is, moreover, peculiar to Elihu to represent God as a teacher both by dreams and dispensations of affliction, <reference osisRef="Job.33.14">Job 33:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.34.32">Job 34:32</reference>, and by His creatures, <reference osisRef="Job.35.11">Job 35:11</reference>; and (3) the designation of God as an incomparable teacher is also not inappropriate here, after His rule is described in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.22">Job 36:22</reference></hi> as transcendently exalted, which on that very account commands to human research a reverence which esteems itself lightly. <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.23">Job 36:23</reference></hi> is not to be translated: who overlooketh Him in His way? (פּקד with על of the personal and <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of the neutral obj.), which is without support in the language; but: who has prescribed to Him (פקד על as <reference osisRef="Job.34.13">Job 34:13</reference>) His way? i.e., as Rosenm. correctly interprets: <hi type="italic">quis ei praescripsit quae agere deberet,</hi> He is no mandatory, is responsible to no one, and under obligation to no one, and who should dare to say (<hi type="italic">quis dixerit;</hi> on the <hi type="italic">perf.</hi> comp. on <reference osisRef="Job.35.15">Job 35:15</reference>): Thou doest evil? - man shall be a docile learner, not a self-satisfied, conceited censurer of the absolute One, whose rule is not to be judged according to the laws of another, but according to His own laws. Thus, then, shall Job remember (<hi type="italic">memento</hi> = <hi type="italic">cura ut</hi>) to extol (תשׂגּיא, <reference osisRef="Job.12.23">Job 12:23</reference>) God’s doings, which have been sung (comp. e.g., <reference osisRef="Ps.104.22">Psa 104:22</reference>) by אנשׁים, men of the right order (<reference osisRef="Job.37.24">Job 37:24</reference>); Jer. <hi type="italic">de quo cecinerunt viri.</hi> שׁרר nowhere has the signification <hi type="italic">intueri</hi> (Rosenm., Umbr.); on the other hand, Elihu is fond of direct (<reference osisRef="Job.33.27">Job 33:27</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.35.10">Job 35:10</reference>) and indirect allusions to the Psalms. All men - he continues, with reference to God’s פּעל, working - behold it, viz., as בו implies, with pleasure and astonishment; mortals gaze upon it (reverentially) from afar, - the same thought as that which has already (<reference osisRef="Job.26.14">Job 26:14</reference>) found the grandest expression in Job’s mouth.
entries.192d7d97f57cb575df34ef7d393f16c8393e118f: Job 36:26-29 26  Behold, God is exalted-we know Him not entirely; <div eID="gen8530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8531" type="x-p"/> The number of His years, it is unsearchable. 27  For He draweth down the drops of water, <div eID="gen8531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8532" type="x-p"/> They distil as rain in connection with its mist, 28  Which the clouds do drop, <div eID="gen8532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8533" type="x-p"/> Distil upon the multitude of men. 29  Who can altogether understand the spreadings of the clouds, <div eID="gen8533" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8534" type="x-p"/> The crash of His tabernacle? <div eID="gen8534" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8535" type="x-p"/> The <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of the quasi-conclusion in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.26">Job 36:26</reference></hi> corresponds to the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of the train of thought in <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.26">Job 36:26</reference></hi> (Ges. §145, 2). מספּר שׁניו is, as the subject-notion, conceived as a nominative (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.4.6">Job 4:6</reference>), not as in similar quasi-antecedent clauses, e.g., <reference osisRef="Job.23.12">Job 23:12</reference>, as an <hi type="italic">acc</hi>. of relation. שׂגּיא here and <reference osisRef="Job.37.23">Job 37:23</reference> occurs otherwise only in Old Testament Chaldee. In what follows Elihu describes the wondrous origin of rain. “If Job had only come,” says a Midrash (<hi type="italic">Jalkut</hi>, §518), “to explain to us the matter of the race of the deluge (vid., especially <reference osisRef="Job.22.15-Job.22.18">Job 22:15-18</reference>), it had been sufficient; and if Elihu had only come to explain to us the matter of the origin of rain (מעשׂה ירידת גשׁמים), it had been enough.” In Gesenius’ <hi type="italic">Handwörterbuch</hi>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.27">Job 36:27</reference> is translated: when He has drawn up the drops of water to Himself, then, etc. But it is יגרע, not גּרע; and גּרע neither in Hebr. nor in Arab. signifies <hi type="italic">attrahere in sublime</hi> (Rosenm.), but only <hi type="italic">attrahere</hi> (root גר) and <hi type="italic">detrahere;</hi> the latter signification is the prevailing one in Hebr. (<reference osisRef="Job.15.8">Job 15:8</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.36.7">Job 36:7</reference>). With כּי the transcendent exaltation of the Being who survives all changes of creation is shown by an example: He draws away (draws off, as it were) the water-drops, viz., from the waters that are confined above on the circle of the sky, which pass over us as mist and cloud (vid., <hi type="italic">Genesis</hi>, S. 107); and these water-drops distil down (זקק, to ooze, distil, here not in a transitive but an intransitive signification, since the water-drops are the rain itself) as rain, לאדו, with its mist, i.e., since a mist produced by it (<reference osisRef="Gen.2.6">Gen 2:6</reference>) fills the expanse (רקיע), the downfall of which is just this rain, which, as <reference osisRef="Job.36.28">Job 36:28</reference> says, the clouds (called שׁחקים on account of its thin strata of air, in distinction from the next mist-circle) cause to flow gently down upon the multitude of men, i.e., far and wide over the mass of men who inhabit the district visited by the rain; both verbs are used transitively here, both נזל as <reference osisRef="Isa.45.8">Isa 45:8</reference>, and רעף, as evidently Pro 3:20. אף אם, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.29">Job 36:29</reference></hi>, commences an intensive question: moreover, could one understand = could one completely understand; which certainly, according to the sense, is equivalent to: how much less (אף כּי). אם is, however, the interrogative <hi type="italic">an</hi>, and אף אם corresponds to האף in the first member of the double question, <reference osisRef="Job.34.17">Job 34:17</reference>; Job 40:8. מפרשׂי are not the burstings, from פּרשׂ = פּרס, <hi type="italic">frangere, findere,</hi> but spreadings, as <reference osisRef="Ezek.27.7">Eze 27:7</reference> shows, from פּרשׂ, <hi type="italic">expandere</hi>, <reference osisRef="Ps.105.39">Psa 105:39</reference>, comp. <hi type="italic">supra</hi> on Job 36:9. It is the growth of the storm-clouds, which collect often from a beginning ”small as a man’s hand” (1Ki 18:44), that is intended; majestic omnipotence conceals itself behind these as in a סכּה (<reference osisRef="Ps.18.12">Psa 18:12</reference>) woven out of thick branches; and the rolling thunder is here called the crash (תּשׁאות, as <reference osisRef="Job.39.7">Job 39:7</reference>, is formed from שׁוא, to rumble, whence also שׁואה, if it is not after the form גּולה, migration, exile, from שׁאה morf ,, vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.30.3">Job 30:3</reference>) of this pavilion of clouds in which the Thunderer works.
entries.76cf324c933ba58085d6e213288f6c5ba57e4d85: <reference osisRef="Job.36.30-Job.33.30">Job 36:30-33 30</reference>  Behold, He spreadeth His light over Himself, <div eID="gen8535" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8536" type="x-p"/> And the roots of the sea He covereth. 31  For thereby He judgeth peoples, <div eID="gen8536" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8537" type="x-p"/> He giveth food in abundance. 32  Both hands He covereth over with light, <div eID="gen8537" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8538" type="x-p"/> And directeth it as one who hitteth the mark. 33  His noise announceth Him, <div eID="gen8538" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8539" type="x-p"/> The cattle even that He is approaching. <div eID="gen8539" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8540" type="x-p"/> A few expositors (Hirz., Hahn, Schlottm.) understand the celestial ocean, or the sea of the upper waters, by ים, <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.30">Job 36:30</reference></hi>; but it is more than questionable (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.9.8">Job 9:8</reference>) whether ים is used anywhere in this sense. Others as (Umbr., Ew.) the masses of water drawn up to the sky out of the depths of the sea, on which a Persian passage cited by Stick. (who, however, regards the <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> of ושׁרשׁי as <hi type="italic">Waw</hi> <hi type="italic">adaequationis</hi>) from Schebisteri may be compared: “an exhalation rises up out of the sea, and comes down at God’s command upon the deserts.” In both cases כּסּה would be equivalent to כסה עליו, <hi type="italic">obtegit se,</hi> which in and of itself is possible. But he who has once witnessed a storm in the neighbourhood of the sea, will decide in favour of one of the three following explanations: (1.) He covereth the uprooted ground of the sea (comp. Psa 18:15.) with the subsiding waves (Blumenf.); but then <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.30">Job 36:30</reference></hi> would require to be understood of the light of the brightening sky following the darkness of the storm, which is improbable in respect of <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.32">Job 36:32</reference></hi>. (2.) While the sky is brilliantly lighted up by the lightning, the abysses of the ocean are veiled in a so much deeper darkness; the observation is correct, but not less so another, that the lightning by a thunder-storm, especially when occurring at night, descends into the depths of the sea like snares that are cast down (פּחים, <reference osisRef="Ps.11.6">Psa 11:6</reference>), and the water is momentarily changed as it were into a sea of flame; accordingly it may be explained, (3.) Behold, He spreadeth over Himself His light (viz., the light which incessantly illumines the world), and the roots of the sea, i.e., the sea down to its depths, He covers with it, since He makes it light through and through (Stuhlm. Wolfs.). Thus, as it appears, Jerome also interprets: <hi type="italic">Et (si voluerit) fulgurare lumine suo desuper, cardines quoque maris operiet.</hi><note placement="foot">The Targ. translates אור, <reference osisRef="Job.36.30">Job 36:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">Job 36:32</reference>, by מטרא, <hi type="italic">pluvia</hi>, according to the erroneous opinion of R. Jochanan: כל אורה שׁנאמר באליהוא אינו אלא בירידת גשׁמים. Aben-Ezra and Kimchi explain even עלי־אור, <reference osisRef="Isa.18.4">Isa 18:4</reference>, according to this passage. The lxx translates <hi type="italic"><reference osisRef="Job.36.30">Job 36:30</reference></hi>: ἰδοὺ ἐκτενεῖ ἐπ ̓ αὐτὸν ἠδώ (<hi type="italic">Cod. Alex.</hi> επ αυτον το τοξον; <hi type="italic">Cod. Sinait.</hi> επ αυτην ηωδη (with the corrections ηδω and τοξον), probably according to the reading אידו for אורו. But what connection have ἠδώ and rainbow?</note> <div eID="gen8540" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen8541" type="x-p"/> This, that He makes the light of the lightning His manifestation (פּרשׂ עליו), and that He covers the earth down to the roots of the sea beneath with this light, is established in <reference osisRef="Job.36.31">Job 36:31</reference> from the design, partly judicial, partly beneficial, which exists in connection with it. בּם refers as neuter (like בּהם, <reference osisRef="Job.22.21">Job 22:21</reference>) to the phenomena of the storm; מכבּיר (with the adverbial ל like לרב, <reference osisRef="Job.26.3">Job 26:3</reference>), what makes great = a making great, abundance (only here), is <hi type="italic">n. hiphil.</hi> after the form משׁהית, <hi type="italic">perdens</hi> = <hi type="italic">perditio</hi>. In <reference osisRef="Job.36.32">Job 36:32</reference> God is represented under a military figure as a slinger of lightnings: He covers light over both hands, i.e., arms both completely with light (comp. סכסך and Arab. <hi type="italic">škk , totum se operire armis</hi>), and directs it (עליה referring to אור as <hi type="italic">fem</hi>. like <reference osisRef="Jer.13.16">Jer 13:16</reference>, and sometimes in the Talmud). But what is the meaning of בּמפגּיע? Hahn takes מפגיע as <hi type="italic">n. hiphil.</hi> like מכביר: an object of attack; but what then becomes of the original <hi type="italic">Hiphil</hi> signification? It ought to be בּמפגּע (<reference osisRef="Job.7.20">Job 7:20</reference>), as Olsh. wishes to read it. Ew., Hirz., and others, after the example of Theod. (lxx), Syr., Jer., translate: against the adversary; מפגיע ;yrasre signifies indeed the opposite in <reference osisRef="Isa.49.16">Isa 49:16</reference> : <hi type="italic">intercessor</hi> (properly, one who assails with prayers); however, it would be possible for this word, just as פגע <hi type="italic">c. acc. </hi>(which signifies usually a hostile meeting, <reference osisRef="Exod.5.3">Exo 5:3</reference> and freq., but sometimes also a friendly, <reference osisRef="Isa.47.3">Isa 47:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Isa.64.4">Isa 64:4</reference>), to be an ἐναντιόσημον. We prefer to abide by the usage of the language as we have it, according to which הפגיע signifies <hi type="italic">facere ut quid incurset s. petat,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.53.6">Isa 53:6</reference>; מפגיע therefore is one who hits, in opposition to one who misses the mark. The <hi type="italic">Beth</hi> is the <hi type="italic">Beth essentiae</hi> (vid., on <reference osisRef="Job.23.13">Job 23:13</reference>), used here like <reference osisRef="Exod.6.3">Exo 6:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.55.19">Psa 55:19</reference>; Isa 40:10. With both hands He seizes the substance of the lightning, fills them with it so that they are completely covered by it, and gives it the command (appoints it its goal), a sure aimer!

                  <ns0:head>CHAP. XXXVI.</ns0:head>
                  <ns0:p n="1">1. ELihu also proceeded, and said,</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="2">2. Suffer me a little <ns0:note n="a" place="bottom">Give me thy patient attention but a little longer, and I have done.</ns0:note>, and I will shew thee <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> that there are yet words for God.</ns0:note> that <ns0:hi>I have</ns0:hi> yet to speak on Gods behalf <ns0:note n="b" place="bottom">That I have not said all that can be said to justifie God's proceedings against thee.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="3">3. I will fetch my knowledge from afar <ns0:note n="c" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> From remote times, and places, and things. I will not confine my discourse to thy particular case, but will justifie God by declaring his great and glorious works of Creation and Providence both in the Heaven and Earth, and the manner of his dealing with men in other Parts and Ages of the World: for these are the chief Heads of the following Discourse, and therefore the best comment upon this general expression.</ns0:note>, and will ascribe righteousness to my Maker <ns0:note n="d" place="bottom">I will acknowledge that which is true, that God is righteous. He adds the words, <ns0:hi>my Maker,</ns0:hi> ei<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ther 1. as an argument or evidence of God's righteousness; partly because it is not likely that God should be unjust to his own Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures, since even men are not only just, but kind to their own Works and Relations: and partly because the Work of Creation gave unto God an absolute right and power to dispose of <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> as he saw fit, as the Potter hath power over the Clay, <ns0:hi>Rom.</ns0:hi> 9. 21. and therefore there was no foundation for unrighteousness, nor any temptation upon God to do it: and partly because Man's Maker must needs be a Being of all possible perfection, and therefore one of perfect righteousness. Or, 2. as a motive or obligation upon him to plead God's cause. I do not engage my self in this Contro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />versie out of a pragmatical or contentious humour, nor out of any prejudice or ill will to thee, but meerly from the sense of my duty to my blessed Creator. Withal he reflects upon <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> as guilty of great folly and ingratitude in contending with him, in or by whom he lived, and moved, and had his being.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="4">4. For truly, my words <ns0:hi>shall</ns0:hi> not <ns0:hi>be</ns0:hi> false <ns0:note n="e" place="bottom">I will not speak any thing against my own Conscience, nor against Truth, either to flatter God, or to vex thee, as thou supposest thy other Friends have done, Chap. 13. 7. and elsewhere.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Ch. 37. 16.</ns0:note> he that is perfect in knowledge <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> with thee <ns0:note n="f" place="bottom">This is meant either 1. of God. Thou hast to do with a God of perfect Knowledge by whom all thy words and actions are weighed; and therefore hast need to be more wary and circumspect in thy expressions and behaviour. Or rather 2. of himself, as the for<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />mer part of the Verse is. And he speaketh of himself in the third Person for modesty's sake. He speaks not of absolute, but of com<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />parative Perfection. And whatsoever perfection of Knowledge he had, he doth not ascribe it to himself but to God's Spirit, Chap. 32. 8. And the meaning may be this, Thou hast not to do with a Novice, but with one who hath accurately considered, and though God's grace doth fully understand these matters. Therefore hearken to me. But the word rendred <ns0:hi>perfect</ns0:hi> signifieth also <ns0:hi>sincere</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>upright,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>right.</ns0:hi> And this may seem best to agree with the former Clause, wherein he saith that he would not speak what he knew to be <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>alse, and now he adds, that he was and would be <ns0:hi>upright</ns0:hi> in the use of his <ns0:hi>knowledge,</ns0:hi> or in the delivery of his <ns0:hi>Opinion</ns0:hi> in this matter, and not be <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                           <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap> by any passion or prejudice either to speak otherwise than he thought, or to judge otherwise than he should.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="5">
                     <ns0:pb facs="tcp:107763:417" />5. Behold, God <ns0:hi>is</ns0:hi> mighty, and despiseth not <ns0:hi>any</ns0:hi> 
                     <ns0:note n="g" place="bottom">His greatness doth not make him (as it doth men) to scorn, or despise, or oppress the meanest. Though he may do what he pleaseth and none can hinder him, yet he will not use it to do any Man wrong, as <ns0:hi>Job</ns0:hi> seemed to in<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                        </ns0:gap>nuate, Chap. 10. 3. & 19. 7. & 23. 13.</ns0:note>: <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 9. 4. & 12. 13, 16. & 37. 23.</ns0:note> 
                     <ns0:hi>he is</ns0:hi> mighty in strength and <ns0:note n="†" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Heb.</ns0:hi> heart.</ns0:note> wisdom. <ns0:note n="h" place="bottom">His strength is guided by Wisdom, and therefore cannot be im<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ployed to do any thing unbecoming God, or unjust to his Crea<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />tures; for either of these is folly. Or, <ns0:hi>in strength,</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>vertue of heart:</ns0:hi> for the <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> is not in the Hebrew. So the sense is, He is truly mag<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />nanimous, of a great and generous mind or heart, and therefore not unrighteous: for all injustice proceeds from littleness or weak<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ness of Heart. Truly great Souls scorn unjust actions.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="6">6. He preserveth not the life of the wicked <ns0:note n="i" place="bottom">To wit, for ever; but will in his due time forsake them, and give them up to the Destroyer. Or, <ns0:hi>he doth not</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>will not preserve</ns0:hi> is put for, <ns0:hi>he will certainly and dreadfully destroy</ns0:hi> by the Figure called <ns0:hi>M<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                              <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap>iosis,</ns0:hi> used <ns0:hi>Prov.</ns0:hi> 17. 21. and oft elsewhere.</ns0:note>: but giveth right to the <ns0:note n="‖" place="margin">
                        <ns0:hi>Or,</ns0:hi> afflicted.</ns0:note> poor <ns0:note n="k" place="bottom">He doth up<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />hold, and he will certainly in his time deliver his poor oppressed Ones from all their Oppressours.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="7">7. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 33. 18. & 34. 15.</ns0:note> He withdraweth not his eyes from the righte<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />ous <ns0:note n="l" place="bottom">He never ceaseth to care for and watch over them, no not when they are afflicted or persecuted, when he may seem to neg<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />lect them.</ns0:note>: but with Kings <ns0:hi>are they</ns0:hi> on the Throne <ns0:note n="m" place="bottom">Though they may be oppressed for a time, yet oft<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />times he not only delivers them, but also raiseth them to the high<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />est Honour and Happiness in this life compare; 1 <ns0:hi>Sam.</ns0:hi> 2. 8. <ns0:hi>Psal.</ns0:hi> 113. 7, 8.</ns0:note>; yea, he doth establish them for ever <ns0:note n="n" place="bottom">Their selicity is more stable and permanent than that of the wicked.</ns0:note>, and they are exalted <ns0:note n="o" place="bottom">Having mentioned the cause, that <ns0:hi>God did esta<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />blish them,</ns0:hi> he now mentions the effect, that <ns0:hi>
                           <ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1 word">
                              <ns0:desc>〈◊〉</ns0:desc>
                           </ns0:gap> are</ns0:hi> or <ns0:hi>continue to be exalted,</ns0:hi> they are not cast down from their Dignity, as the wicked commonly are.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="8">8. And <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Psal. 107. 10.</ns0:note> if <ns0:hi>they be</ns0:hi> bound in fetters <ns0:note n="p" place="bottom">If through the vicissitude of Worldly affairs, and the righteous judgment of God upon them for their sins they be brought from their Throne into a Prison, as sometimes hath been done.</ns0:note>, <ns0:hi>and</ns0:hi> be holden in cords of affliction:</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="9">9. Then he sheweth them their work <ns0:note n="q" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> Their evil works, as the next Clause explains and limits it. By these afflictions he brings them to a sight of their sins and to repentance, which is the way and means of their recovery.</ns0:note>, and their transgressions, that they have exceeded <ns0:note n="r" place="bottom">That they have greatly sinned by abusing their Power and Prosperity, which even good men are too prone to do.</ns0:note>.</ns0:p>
                  <ns0:p n="10">10. <ns0:note n="*" place="margin">Chap. 33. 16.</ns0:note> He openeth also their ear <ns0:note n="s" place="bottom">
                        <ns0:hi>i. e.</ns0:hi> He enableth and enclineth them to hearken to what God speaks by the rod, who would not hear in the time of their Pro<ns0:g ref="char:EOLhyphen" />sperity, like them; <ns0:hi>Jer.</ns0:hi> 22. 21.</ns0:note> to discipline <ns0:note n="t" place="bottom">Or, <ns0:hi>to instruction,</ns0:hi> i. e. to receive instruction: or <ns0:hi>to chastening,</ns0:hi> i. e. to hear the rod, and who hath appointed it, as is said, <ns0:hi>Mich.</ns0:hi> 6. 9.</ns0:note>, and commandeth <ns0:note n="u" place="bottom">Either by his Word o<ns0:gap reason="illegible" resp="#APEX" extent="1+ letters">
                           <ns0:desc>•…</ns0:desc>
